The meaning of ﴿above it﴾ is that they are elevated over it, because they are parts of the earth, and they differ from it only in respect of elevation, so in this respect they are as though distinct from it.

﴿And He blessed in it﴾: meaning He made it blessed, abundant in good, by what He created in it of benefits for the servants.

Al-Suddi said: He made its trees grow. ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾. Qatada and Mujahid said: He created in it its rivers, its trees and its animals. Al-Hasan, Ikrima and al-Dahhak said: He measured in it the provisions of its people and what suits their livelihoods, from trades, trees and benefits. He placed in each land what He did not place in the other, so that some of them might live from others through trade and travel from one land to another. The meaning of ﴿in four days﴾: meaning, in completion of four days together with the two days preceding. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others.

Ibn al-Anbari said: an example of this is the statement of a speaker: "I went from Basra to Baghdad in ten days, and to Kufa in fifteen days," meaning: in completion of fifteen days. So the meaning is that the occurrence of all that preceded, from the creation of the earth and what follows it, was in four days.

The accusative of *sawaan* (سَواءً) is an emphatic infinitive (*maşdar mu'akkid*, an emphasizing verbal noun) for an omitted verb. It is an adjective describing "days," meaning: they became equal (*istawat sawaan*), in the sense of *istiwa'an* (equally, evenly). It may also be in the accusative of circumstance (*hal*) relating to "the earth" or to the pronouns referring to it.

Ibn Kathir's reading... (omitted)

The majority of readers recited *sawaan* in the accusative. Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Ya'qub and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd recited it in the genitive, making it an adjective of *ayyam* (days). Abu Ja'far recited it in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "in four days, complete and equal," and the phrase *lil-sa'ilin* (لِلسَّائِلِينَ, "for those who ask") is connected to *sawaan*, meaning "equal for those who ask." Or it is connected to an omitted element, as if it were said: "This restriction is for those who ask, 'How long was the earth and what is in it created?'" Or it is connected to *qaddara* (قَدَّرَ, "He measured"), meaning: He measured in it its sustenance for the seekers who are in need of it.

Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the sentence, and the meaning is: "He measured in it its sustenance, equal for those in need, in four days." Ibn Jarir chose this view.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the creation of the earth and what is in it, He mentioned the manner of His creating the heavens. So He said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, meaning He purposed and directed Himself toward it with a straight intention.

Al-Razi said: it is from their saying *istawa ila makan kadha* ("he went straight to such a place") when one directs oneself to it in such a way that he does not turn toward any other task. It is from *al-istiwa'* (straightness), which is the opposite of crookedness. Its parallel is their saying *istaqama ilayhi* ("he proceeded straight toward it"), and from it the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So go straight to Him﴾. The meaning is: then the caller of wisdom called Him to create the heavens after creating the earth and what is in it.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is that His command ascended to the heaven while it was smoke. *Al-dukhan* (الدُّخانُ, "smoke") is what rises from the flame of fire, and it is used metaphorically for what is seen as vapor from the earth.

The exegetes said: this smoke is the vapor of water. Allah, exalted is He, specified the *istiwa'* toward the heaven, although the address that follows is directed to both it and the earth, as His saying indicates: ﴿He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly."﴾ This is done with reliance on what was previously mentioned of their measuring and the measuring of what is in them. The meaning of *i'tiya* (ائْتِيا, "come") is: do what I command you and come with it, just as one says *i'ti ma huwa al-ahsan* ("bring what is best"), meaning: do it.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said that Allah, exalted is He, said: "As for you, O heaven, bring forth your sun, your moon and your stars. As for you, O earth, split your rivers, bring forth your fruits and your plants."

The majority recited ﴿ائْتِيا﴾ as an imperative from *al-ityan* (coming). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid recited *atiya qalata atayna* with a long vowel (madd) in both places. It is either from *al-mu'atah* (مُؤَاتَاةِ), which is agreement, meaning that each of you should agree with the other, or from *al-iyta'* (الإيتاءِ), which is giving. Its pattern according to the first is *fa'ila* like *qatila*, and according to the second *af'ila* like *akrima*. ﴿Willingly or unwillingly﴾: both are verbal nouns in the position of circumstance, meaning obedient or compelled. Al-A'mash recited *kurhan* with a *damma*.

Al-Zajjaj said: obey obediently, or be compelled into compliance.

It was said: the meaning of this command to them is subjugation, that is: be, and they were, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl 16:40]. The speech is therefore a figure of speech demonstrating the effect of His power and the impossibility of their refusal. ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾ meaning: we come to your command submissively. He combined them in the plural of the rational, because He addressed them with what is addressed to rational beings.

Al-Qurtubi said: most scholars said that Allah, exalted is He, created speech in them, so they spoke as He willed, exalted is He. It was also said that this is an illustration of the manifestation of obedience from them and the effect of the Lordly power upon them.

﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾, meaning He created them, perfected them and finished with them, as in the verse of the poet:

*And upon them two coats of mail, which Dawud completed,*
*or which the maker of the flowing coats, Tubba', made.*

The pronoun in *qada-hunna* (قَضاهُنَّ) either refers to the heaven according to its meaning, since it is seven heavens, or it is an ambiguous pronoun explained by *seven heavens*. The accusative of *sab'a samawat* is either an explanation (*tafsir*) or a substitution (*badal*) of the pronoun.

It was said that its accusative is as the second object of *qada-hunna*, because it is implicitly meaning "making them." It was said it is an accusative of circumstance, meaning: He completed them while they were numbered as seven. Then *qada* means *sana'a* (made). It was also said that it is an accusative of specification (*tamyiz*). The meaning of *fi yawmayn* (في يَوْمَيْنِ, "in two days") is as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾, so the total is six days, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-A'raf 7:3]. Its explanation was previously given in Surat al-A'raf.

Mujahid said: one day of the six days is like a thousand years of what you count.

'Abd Allah ibn Salam said: He created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and measured in it its sustenance on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens on Thursday and Friday.

His saying ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾ is conjoined to *qada-hunna*.

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: meaning He created in it its sun, its moon, its stars, its orbits, and what is in them of angels, seas, hail and snow.

It was said: the meaning is that He inspired in them what He willed and what He commanded. Revelation (*al-iha'*) may also mean command, as in His saying: ﴿That your Lord has revealed to it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:5], and His saying: ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:111], meaning: I commanded them.

The combination of this verse with His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:30] has been considered problematic, since what is in this verse, "Then He turned to the heaven," indicates that its creation was later than the creation of the earth, and its apparent meaning contradicts His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾. It was said that the *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") in ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ is not for temporal sequence but for sequence of rank (*rutbi*), and the problem is thus resolved from its root. Even if it is for temporal sequence, the combination is possible: the creation of the earth precedes the creation of the heaven, and its spreading (*dahw*), meaning its extension, is an additional matter beyond the mere creation of it. So it is previously created but later spread out. This is apparent. Perhaps further clarification of the matter will come when we explain His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾, God willing.

﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾, meaning with shining, glittering stars upon it, like the glitter of lamps. The accusative of *hifzan* (حِفْظًا, "as protection") is either a verbal noun emphasizing an omitted verb, meaning: and We protected them with protection, or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), on the assumption: and We created the lamps as adornment and protection. The first is preferable.

Abu Hayyan said: the second view is a strain and a departure from what is simple and clear. The protection meant is protecting the heaven from the devils who steal hearing. The reference in His saying *dhalika* (ذَلِكَ, "that") is to what has been mentioned. ﴿The decree of the Mighty, the Knowing﴾, meaning the one most capable and most knowing.

﴿But if they turn away﴾ from reflection and contemplation upon these creatures, ﴿then say: "I have warned you"﴾, meaning: then say to them, O Muhammad, "I have warned you, I have frightened you, ﴿of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾," meaning a punishment like their punishment. The intended meaning of *al-sa'iqa* (الصَّاعِقَةُ, "thunderbolt") is destructive punishment of every kind.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-sa'iqa* is the destroying blow, whatever it may be.

The majority recited *sa'iqatan* (صاعِقَةً) in both places with an *alif*. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Nakha'i, al-Sulami and Ibn Muhaysin recited *sa'qatan* (صَعْقَةً) in both places. The meaning of *al-sa'iqa* and *al-sa'qa* was previously explained in al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿when the messengers came to them﴾ is a temporal clause (*zarf*) modifying either ﴿I have warned you﴾ or *sa'iqatan*, because it means punishment. That is: "I have warned you of the punishment that fell at the time when the messengers came." Or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the thunderbolt of 'Ad.

This is preferable to the first two views, because the warning did not occur at the time the messengers came, so it cannot correctly be a temporal clause for it. Likewise, the thunderbolt cannot correctly have that time as its temporal clause.

His saying ﴿from before them and from behind them﴾ is connected to *jaa'at-hum* (came to them), meaning: they came to them from all their sides. It was also said the meaning is: the messengers who came before and after came to them, by treating the arrival of their speech as the arrival of themselves, as if the messengers had come to them and addressed them with their saying: ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾, meaning: that you not worship. *Anna* here is the verbal (*masdariyya*) particle. It may also be the explanatory (*tafsiriyya*) particle, or the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, whose noun is an omitted pronoun of matter (*dhamir sha'n*).

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned their reply to the messengers, and said: ﴿They said: "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels"﴾, meaning: He would have sent them to us, and He did not send to us a human being of our kind.

Then they openly declared disbelief without hesitation, and said: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾, meaning: we disbelieve in what you claim, that Allah sent you to us, because you are human beings like us with no superiority over us. So how did He single you out with His message rather than us? The reply to this feeble doubt, which they raised, has already been given in more than one place.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat﴾ that he said: they do not testify that there is no god but Allah. And concerning His saying: ﴿For them is a reward never to be cut off﴾, he said: never to be diminished.

Ibn Jarir and al-Nahhas in his *Nasikh*, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from him that: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about the creation of the heavens and the earth. He said: Allah created the earth on Sunday and Monday, created the mountains and what is in them of benefits on Tuesday, and on Wednesday He created trees, stone, water, cities, civilization and ruin. These are four days. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: 'Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and you set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds.' He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask﴾. And He created the heaven on Thursday, and created on Friday the stars, the sun, the moon and the angels, until three hours remained of it. In the first of these three hours He created the terms of life, when each one who dies dies. In the second He cast into it everything of benefit. In the third He created Adam, settled him in the Garden, commanded Iblis to prostrate to him, and expelled him from it in the last hour." The Jews said: "Then what, O Muhammad?" He said: "Then He established Himself upon the Throne." They said: "You have been right, had you completed it." They said: "Then He rested." The Prophet (ﷺ) became very angry, and then there was revealed: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Qaf 50:38–39].

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, concerning His saying ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾, that he said: He split the rivers, planted the trees, set the mountains, made the seas flow, and placed in this what is not in that, and in that what is not in this.

Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him, saying: Allah, exalted is He, created a day and named it Sunday, then created a second and named it Monday, then created a third and named it Tuesday, then created a fourth and named it Wednesday, then created a fifth and named it Thursday, and he mentioned something similar to what was previously mentioned.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah finished His creation in six days," and he mentioned something similar to what was previously mentioned.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Bakr something similar to what was previously narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ that he said: He said to the heaven: "Bring forth your sun, your moon and your stars," and to the earth: "Split your rivers and bring forth your fruits." ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying *i'tiya* (ائْتِيا): he said, "Give." And concerning His saying *ataina* (أتَيْنا): he said, "We gave."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verses 2–14 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan by the consensus of all scholars. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that it was revealed in Mecca. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi (both in al-Dala'il), and Ibn Asakir narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: "Quraysh gathered one day and said: 'Look for the most knowledgeable of you in sorcery, soothsaying and poetry, and let him go to this man who has divided our community, scattered our affairs and reviled our religion. Let him speak to him and see what he replies.' They said: 'We know of no one except Utba ibn Rabi'a.' So they said: 'Go, O Abu al-Walid.' He went to him and said: 'O Muhammad, are you better, or Abd Allah? Are you better, or Abd al-Muttalib?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was silent. He said: 'If you claim that these are better than you, then they worshipped the gods you have reviled. And if you claim that you are better than them, then speak, so that we may hear your words. By Allah, we have never seen a young shoot more ill-omened for your people than you. You have divided our community, scattered our affairs, reviled our religion and disgraced us among the Arabs, until word has spread among them that there is a sorcerer in Quraysh and a soothsayer in Quraysh. By Allah, we are only waiting for a cry like that of a woman in labour, that some of us will rise against others with swords. O man, if what you want is wealth, we will gather for you so that you become the richest man of Quraysh. And if what you want is women, choose whichever women of Quraysh you wish, and we will marry you to ten of them.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Have you finished?' He said: 'Yes.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. A Book whose verses are made clear…' until he reached: '…But if they turn away, then say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd.' [Fussilat: 1–13]. Utba said: 'Enough, enough! Do you have anything other than this?' He said: 'No.' So he returned to Quraysh, and they said: 'What is behind you?' He said: 'I did not leave anything that I thought you would speak to him about except that I spoke to him about it.' They said: 'Did he answer you?' He said: 'By the One who raised it as a structure, I did not understand anything of what he said, except that he warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd.' They said: 'Woe to you! A man speaks to you in Arabic and you do not know what he said?' He said: 'No, by Allah, I did not understand anything of what he said except the mention of the thunderbolt.'"

Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi (both in al-Dala'il) narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to Utba ibn Rabi'a: 'Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,' he went to his companions and said: 'O people, obey me in this matter today, and disobey me after it. By Allah, I have heard from this man words that my ears have never heard the like of, and I do not know what he meant by them.'"

There are narrations on this subject indicating that Quraysh gathered, sent Utba ibn Rabi'a, and that he recited to him the beginning of this surah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His statement: ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾. The discussion of its i'rab (grammatical analysis) and its meaning has already preceded in the surah before this one, so we do not repeat it.

Likewise, the discussion of the meaning of ﴿tanzīl﴾ (revelation) and its i'rab has already preceded.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash said: ﴿Tanzīl﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿a Book whose verses are made clear﴾. Al-Farra' said: It is permissible that it be by supposing a hidden [predicate] of this, and it is also permissible to say that ﴿a Book﴾ is an appositive (badal) of ﴿tanzīl﴾, and ﴿from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is connected to ﴿tanzīl﴾.

The meaning of ﴿whose verses are made clear﴾ is: they are explained, or made into varied styles. Qatada said: They are made clear by explaining its lawful from its unlawful, and obedience from disobedience. Al-Hasan said: By promise and threat. Sufyan said: By reward and punishment. There is no barrier to applying it to all of these.

The clause is in the accusative position as a description (ṣifah) of ﴿a Book﴾. It was also read as ﴿fuṣilat﴾ with lightened pronunciation, meaning: it distinguished between truth and falsehood. The accusative of ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: its verses were made clear while it was an Arabic Qur'an.

Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative for praise. It was said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: he recites it as a Qur'an. It was said: it is a second object of ﴿fuṣilat﴾. It was said: it is by a hidden verb indicated by ﴿fuṣilat﴾, meaning: We made it clear as an Arabic Qur'an. ﴿For a people who know﴾ means: they know its meanings and understand them, and they are the people of the Arabic tongue.

Al-Dahhak said: meaning, they know that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah.

Mujahid said: meaning, they know that He is one God in the Torah and the Gospel. The lam is connected to a deleted element, as another description of ﴿Qur'an﴾, meaning: existing for a people; or it is connected to ﴿fuṣilat﴾. The first is preferable.

Likewise ﴿a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ are two other descriptions of ﴿Qur'an﴾, or two circumstantial states of ﴿a Book﴾. The meaning: a bringer of good tidings to the friends of Allah and a warner to His enemies.

It was also read as ﴿bashīrun wa-nadhīrun﴾ in the nominative, as descriptions of ﴿a Book﴾, or as predicates of a deleted subject.

﴿But most of them turned away﴾: by "most" here is meant the disbelievers, meaning: the disbelievers turned away from what it contained of warning. ﴿So they do not hear﴾: a hearing by which they benefit, because of their turning away from it.

﴿And they say: our hearts are in coverings﴾: meaning, in wrappings like a quiver in which arrows are kept, so it does not understand what you say, and your speech does not reach it. The word ﴿akinna﴾ is the plural of ﴿kinān﴾, which is a covering. Mujahid said: the kinān for the heart is like the shield for the arrow. The explanation of this has already preceded in al-Baqarah. ﴿And in our ears is a heaviness﴾: meaning deafness; the root of waqr is heaviness.

Talha ibn Musarrif read ﴿wiqr﴾ with a kasrah on the waw, and it was also read with a fatḥah on the waw and the qaf. The ﴿min﴾ in ﴿and between us and between you there is a barrier﴾ is for the beginning of the limit. The meaning: the barrier began from us and began from you, so the intermediate space between our direction and your direction is filled with the barrier, with no empty gap in it. These are images of the dullness of their hearts in grasping the truth, the rejection of their ears for it, and the impossibility of connection between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾: meaning, act according to your religion, indeed we act according to our religion.

Al-Kalbi said: act for our destruction, for indeed we act for your destruction. Muqatil said: act for your God who sent you, for indeed we act for our gods that we worship. It was said: act for your Hereafter, for indeed we act for our worldly life.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to answer their statement, and He said: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me that your God is one God﴾. Meaning: I am only like one of you, were it not for the revelation, and I am not of a different kind from you, such that your hearts would be in coverings from what I call you to, and in your ears a heaviness, and between me and you a barrier. I have not called you to what opposes reason; rather, I call you to monotheism. The majority read ﴿yūḥā﴾ in the passive. Al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i read it in the active, meaning: Allah reveals to me.

It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: I am not able to compel you to faith by force. I am a human being like you, and I have no distinction over you except that monotheism and the command to it are revealed to me. So upon me is only the delivery; if you accept, you will be guided, and if you refuse, you will be destroyed.

It was also said: the meaning is: I am not an angel; I am only a human being like you, and it has been revealed to me apart from you. So by revelation I became a prophet, and it became obligatory upon you to follow me.

Al-Hasan said concerning the meaning of the verse: Allah, glory be to Him, taught His Messenger (ﷺ) how to be humble.

﴿So go straight to Him﴾: it is transitive with ﴿ilā﴾ because it includes the meaning of "turn towards." The meaning: direct your uprightness to Him by obedience, do not incline away from His path, and seek His forgiveness for the sins that have passed from you.

Then He threatened and warned the polytheists, and said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾.

Then He described them by His statement: ﴿Who do not give zakāh﴾: meaning they withhold it and do not bring it out to the poor.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: they do not acknowledge its obligation.

Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: they do not give charity and do not spend in obedience.

It was said: the meaning of the verse is: they do not testify that there is no god but Allah, because that is the zakāh (purification) of souls and their cleansing.

Al-Farra' said: the polytheists used to spend expenses, give drink to the pilgrims and feed them, so they forbade that to whoever believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed concerning them.

﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿do not give﴾ and is included with it within the scope of the relative clause, meaning: they deny the Hereafter and reject it. The bringing of the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) is for the purpose of restriction.

﴿Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is a reward never cut off﴾: meaning, not cut off from them. It is said: "I cut the rope" (mannantu al-ḥabl) when you severed it. From this is the statement of al-Asbagh al-Azdi:

"By your life, I do not refuse, with a single bond, to a friend, nor is my goodness cut off."

It was also said: al-mamnūn means the diminished. Qutrub said this, and he recited the statement of Zuhayr:

"The superiority of the swift over the slow horses, so he does not give with it anything diminished or hasty."

Al-Jawhari said: al-mann is cutting, and it is said to mean reduction, and from it is the statement of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿for them is a reward never diminished﴾. Labid said:

"Dun-coloured, sharp-clawed, its food is not cut off."

Mujahid said: ﴿never cut off﴾ means: not counted. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: it is not bestowed upon them as a favour, because a favour is bestowed as grace, but as for the reward, its payment is a due right.

Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the sick, the disabled and the elderly, that when they become too weak for obedience, there is recorded for them the reward of what they used to do when they were in their best health.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to rebuke and reprimand them, and He said: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days?﴾ Meaning: do you disbelieve in the One whose matter is this great matter and whose power is this overwhelming power?

It was said: the two days are Sunday and Monday. It was said: what is meant is the measure of two days, because the true day only comes into being after the existence of the earth and the heaven.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿a-innakum﴾ with two hamzahs, the second between-between (bayna bayna, an intermediate sound). Ibn Kathir read it with one hamzah followed by a light yā'.

﴿And you set up rivals to Him﴾: meaning, equals and partners. The clause is conjoined to ﴿you disbelieve﴾ and falls under the interrogation. The reference with His statement ﴿that﴾ to the relative pronoun characterised by what has been mentioned is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. And among the worlds is what you set up as rivals to Allah. So how do you make some of His creatures partners with Him in worship?

His statement: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains﴾ is conjoined to ﴿created﴾, meaning: how do you disbelieve in the One who created the earth and placed in it firm mountains, meaning: firm mountains above it. It was said: the clause ﴿and He placed in it firm mountains﴾ is a new sentence, not conjoined to ﴿created﴾, because the separation between them is by something foreign.

The first is preferable, because the separating clause confirms the content of what came before it, so it has the status of emphasis. The meaning of ﴿above it﴾ is that they are elevated over it, because they are parts of the earth, and they differ from it only in respect of elevation, so in this respect they are as though distinct from it.

﴿And He blessed in it﴾: meaning He made it blessed, abundant in good, by what He created in it of benefits for the servants.

Al-Suddi said: He made its trees grow. ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾. Qatada and Mujahid said: He created in it its rivers, its trees and its animals. Al-Hasan, Ikrima and al-Dahhak said: He measured in it the provisions of its people and what suits their livelihoods, from trades, trees and benefits. He placed in each land what He did not place in the other, so that some of them might live from others through trade and travel from one land to another. The meaning of ﴿in four days﴾: meaning, in completion of four days together with the two days preceding. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others.

Ibn al-Anbari said: an example of this is the statement of a speaker: "I went from Basra to Baghdad in ten days, and to Kufa in fifteen days," meaning: in completion of fifteen days. So the meaning is that the occurrence of all that preceded, from the creation of the earth and what follows it, was in four days.

The accusative of *sawaan* (سَواءً) is an emphatic infinitive (*maşdar mu'akkid*, an emphasizing verbal noun) for an omitted verb. It is an adjective describing "days," meaning: they became equal (*istawat sawaan*), in the sense of *istiwa'an* (equally, evenly). It may also be in the accusative of circumstance (*hal*) relating to "the earth" or to the pronouns referring to it.

Ibn Kathir's reading... (omitted)

The majority of readers recited *sawaan* in the accusative. Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Ya'qub and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd recited it in the genitive, making it an adjective of *ayyam* (days). Abu Ja'far recited it in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "in four days, complete and equal," and the phrase *lil-sa'ilin* (لِلسَّائِلِينَ, "for those who ask") is connected to *sawaan*, meaning "equal for those who ask." Or it is connected to an omitted element, as if it were said: "This restriction is for those who ask, 'How long was the earth and what is in it created?'" Or it is connected to *qaddara* (قَدَّرَ, "He measured"), meaning: He measured in it its sustenance for the seekers who are in need of it.

Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the sentence, and the meaning is: "He measured in it its sustenance, equal for those in need, in four days." Ibn Jarir chose this view.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the creation of the earth and what is in it, He mentioned the manner of His creating the heavens. So He said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, meaning He purposed and directed Himself toward it with a straight intention.

Al-Razi said: it is from their saying *istawa ila makan kadha* ("he went straight to such a place") when one directs oneself to it in such a way that he does not turn toward any other task. It is from *al-istiwa'* (straightness), which is the opposite of crookedness. Its parallel is their saying *istaqama ilayhi* ("he proceeded straight toward it"), and from it the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So go straight to Him﴾. The meaning is: then the caller of wisdom called Him to create the heavens after creating the earth and what is in it.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is that His command ascended to the heaven while it was smoke. *Al-dukhan* (الدُّخانُ, "smoke") is what rises from the flame of fire, and it is used metaphorically for what is seen as vapor from the earth.

The exegetes said: this smoke is the vapor of water. Allah, exalted is He, specified the *istiwa'* toward the heaven, although the address that follows is directed to both it and the earth, as His saying indicates: ﴿He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly."﴾ This is done with reliance on what was previously mentioned of their measuring and the measuring of what is in them. The meaning of *i'tiya* (ائْتِيا, "come") is: do what I command you and come with it, just as one says *i'ti ma huwa al-ahsan* ("bring what is best"), meaning: do it.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said that Allah, exalted is He, said: "As for you, O heaven, bring forth your sun, your moon and your stars. As for you, O earth, split your rivers, bring forth your fruits and your plants."

The majority recited ﴿ائْتِيا﴾ as an imperative from *al-ityan* (coming). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid recited *atiya qalata atayna* with a long vowel (madd) in both places. It is either from *al-mu'atah* (مُؤَاتَاةِ), which is agreement, meaning that each of you should agree with the other, or from *al-iyta'* (الإيتاءِ), which is giving. Its pattern according to the first is *fa'ila* like *qatila*, and according to the second *af'ila* like *akrima*. ﴿Willingly or unwillingly﴾: both are verbal nouns in the position of circumstance, meaning obedient or compelled. Al-A'mash recited *kurhan* with a *damma*.

Al-Zajjaj said: obey obediently, or be compelled into compliance.

It was said: the meaning of this command to them is subjugation, that is: be, and they were, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl 16:40]. The speech is therefore a figure of speech demonstrating the effect of His power and the impossibility of their refusal. ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾ meaning: we come to your command submissively. He combined them in the plural of the rational, because He addressed them with what is addressed to rational beings.

Al-Qurtubi said: most scholars said that Allah, exalted is He, created speech in them, so they spoke as He willed, exalted is He. It was also said that this is an illustration of the manifestation of obedience from them and the effect of the Lordly power upon them.

﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾, meaning He created them, perfected them and finished with them, as in the verse of the poet:

*And upon them two coats of mail, which Dawud completed,*
*or which the maker of the flowing coats, Tubba', made.*

The pronoun in *qada-hunna* (قَضاهُنَّ) either refers to the heaven according to its meaning, since it is seven heavens, or it is an ambiguous pronoun explained by *seven heavens*. The accusative of *sab'a samawat* is either an explanation (*tafsir*) or a substitution (*badal*) of the pronoun.

It was said that its accusative is as the second object of *qada-hunna*, because it is implicitly meaning "making them." It was said it is an accusative of circumstance, meaning: He completed them while they were numbered as seven. Then *qada* means *sana'a* (made). It was also said that it is an accusative of specification (*tamyiz*). The meaning of *fi yawmayn* (في يَوْمَيْنِ, "in two days") is as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾, so the total is six days, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-A'raf 7:3]. Its explanation was previously given in Surat al-A'raf.

Mujahid said: one day of the six days is like a thousand years of what you count.

'Abd Allah ibn Salam said: He created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and measured in it its sustenance on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens on Thursday and Friday.

His saying ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾ is conjoined to *qada-hunna*.

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: meaning He created in it its sun, its moon, its stars, its orbits, and what is in them of angels, seas, hail and snow.

It was said: the meaning is that He inspired in them what He willed and what He commanded. Revelation (*al-iha'*) may also mean command, as in His saying: ﴿That your Lord has revealed to it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:5], and His saying: ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:111], meaning: I commanded them.

The combination of this verse with His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:30] has been considered problematic, since what is in this verse, "Then He turned to the heaven," indicates that its creation was later than the creation of the earth, and its apparent meaning contradicts His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾. It was said that the *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") in ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ is not for temporal sequence but for sequence of rank (*rutbi*), and the problem is thus resolved from its root. Even if it is for temporal sequence, the combination is possible: the creation of the earth precedes the creation of the heaven, and its spreading (*dahw*), meaning its extension, is an additional matter beyond the mere creation of it. So it is previously created but later spread out. This is apparent. Perhaps further clarification of the matter will come when we explain His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾, God willing.

﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾, meaning with shining, glittering stars upon it, like the glitter of lamps. The accusative of *hifzan* (حِفْظًا, "as protection") is either a verbal noun emphasizing an omitted verb, meaning: and We protected them with protection, or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), on the assumption: and We created the lamps as adornment and protection. The first is preferable.

Abu Hayyan said: the second view is a strain and a departure from what is simple and clear. The protection meant is protecting the heaven from the devils who steal hearing. The reference in His saying *dhalika* (ذَلِكَ, "that") is to what has been mentioned. ﴿The decree of the Mighty, the Knowing﴾, meaning the one most capable and most knowing.

﴿But if they turn away﴾ from reflection and contemplation upon these creatures, ﴿then say: "I have warned you"﴾, meaning: then say to them, O Muhammad, "I have warned you, I have frightened you, ﴿of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾," meaning a punishment like their punishment. The intended meaning of *al-sa'iqa* (الصَّاعِقَةُ, "thunderbolt") is destructive punishment of every kind.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-sa'iqa* is the destroying blow, whatever it may be.

The majority recited *sa'iqatan* (صاعِقَةً) in both places with an *alif*. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Nakha'i, al-Sulami and Ibn Muhaysin recited *sa'qatan* (صَعْقَةً) in both places. The meaning of *al-sa'iqa* and *al-sa'qa* was previously explained in al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿when the messengers came to them﴾ is a temporal clause (*zarf*) modifying either ﴿I have warned you﴾ or *sa'iqatan*, because it means punishment. That is: "I have warned you of the punishment that fell at the time when the messengers came." Or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the thunderbolt of 'Ad.

This is preferable to the first two views, because the warning did not occur at the time the messengers came, so it cannot correctly be a temporal clause for it. Likewise, the thunderbolt cannot correctly have that time as its temporal clause.

His saying ﴿from before them and from behind them﴾ is connected to *jaa'at-hum* (came to them), meaning: they came to them from all their sides. It was also said the meaning is: the messengers who came before and after came to them, by treating the arrival of their speech as the arrival of themselves, as if the messengers had come to them and addressed them with their saying: ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾, meaning: that you not worship. *Anna* here is the verbal (*masdariyya*) particle. It may also be the explanatory (*tafsiriyya*) particle, or the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, whose noun is an omitted pronoun of matter (*dhamir sha'n*).

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned their reply to the messengers, and said: ﴿They said: "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels"﴾, meaning: He would have sent them to us, and He did not send to us a human being of our kind.

Then they openly declared disbelief without hesitation, and said: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾, meaning: we disbelieve in what you claim, that Allah sent you to us, because you are human beings like us with no superiority over us. So how did He single you out with His message rather than us? The reply to this feeble doubt, which they raised, has already been given in more than one place.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat﴾ that he said: they do not testify that there is no god but Allah. And concerning His saying: ﴿For them is a reward never to be cut off﴾, he said: never to be diminished.

Ibn Jarir and al-Nahhas in his *Nasikh*, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from him that: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about the creation of the heavens and the earth. He said: Allah created the earth on Sunday and Monday, created the mountains and what is in them of benefits on Tuesday, and on Wednesday He created trees, stone, water, cities, civilization and ruin. These are four days. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: 'Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and you set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds.' He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask﴾. And He created the heaven on Thursday, and created on Friday the stars, the sun, the moon and the angels, until three hours remained of it. In the first of these three hours He created the terms of life, when each one who dies dies. In the second He cast into it everything of benefit. In the third He created Adam, settled him in the Garden, commanded Iblis to prostrate to him, and expelled him from it in the last hour." The Jews said: "Then what, O Muhammad?" He said: "Then He established Himself upon the Throne." They said: "You have been right, had you completed it." They said: "Then He rested." The Prophet (ﷺ) became very angry, and then there was revealed: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Qaf 50:38–39].

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, concerning His saying ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾, that he said: He split the rivers, planted the trees, set the mountains, made the seas flow, and placed in this what is not in that, and in that what is not in this.

Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him, saying: Allah, exalted is He, created a day and named it Sunday, then created a second and named it Monday, then created a third and named it Tuesday, then created a fourth and named it Wednesday, then created a fifth and named it Thursday, and he mentioned something similar to what was previously mentioned.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah finished His creation in six days," and he mentioned something similar to what was previously mentioned.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Bakr something similar to what was previously narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ that he said: He said to the heaven: "Bring forth your sun, your moon and your stars," and to the earth: "Split your rivers and bring forth your fruits." ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying *i'tiya* (ائْتِيا): he said, "Give." And concerning His saying *ataina* (أتَيْنا): he said, "We gave."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verses 2–14 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan by the consensus of all scholars. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that it was revealed in Mecca. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi (both in al-Dala'il), and Ibn Asakir narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: "Quraysh gathered one day and said: 'Look for the most knowledgeable of you in sorcery, soothsaying and poetry, and let him go to this man who has divided our community, scattered our affairs and reviled our religion. Let him speak to him and see what he replies.' They said: 'We know of no one except Utba ibn Rabi'a.' So they said: 'Go, O Abu al-Walid.' He went to him and said: 'O Muhammad, are you better, or Abd Allah? Are you better, or Abd al-Muttalib?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was silent. He said: 'If you claim that these are better than you, then they worshipped the gods you have reviled. And if you claim that you are better than them, then speak, so that we may hear your words. By Allah, we have never seen a young shoot more ill-omened for your people than you. You have divided our community, scattered our affairs, reviled our religion and disgraced us among the Arabs, until word has spread among them that there is a sorcerer in Quraysh and a soothsayer in Quraysh. By Allah, we are only waiting for a cry like that of a woman in labour, that some of us will rise against others with swords. O man, if what you want is wealth, we will gather for you so that you become the richest man of Quraysh. And if what you want is women, choose whichever women of Quraysh you wish, and we will marry you to ten of them.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Have you finished?' He said: 'Yes.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. A Book whose verses are made clear…' until he reached: '…But if they turn away, then say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd.' [Fussilat: 1–13]. Utba said: 'Enough, enough! Do you have anything other than this?' He said: 'No.' So he returned to Quraysh, and they said: 'What is behind you?' He said: 'I did not leave anything that I thought you would speak to him about except that I spoke to him about it.' They said: 'Did he answer you?' He said: 'By the One who raised it as a structure, I did not understand anything of what he said, except that he warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd.' They said: 'Woe to you! A man speaks to you in Arabic and you do not know what he said?' He said: 'No, by Allah, I did not understand anything of what he said except the mention of the thunderbolt.'"

Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi (both in al-Dala'il) narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to Utba ibn Rabi'a: 'Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,' he went to his companions and said: 'O people, obey me in this matter today, and disobey me after it. By Allah, I have heard from this man words that my ears have never heard the like of, and I do not know what he meant by them.'"

There are narrations on this subject indicating that Quraysh gathered, sent Utba ibn Rabi'a, and that he recited to him the beginning of this surah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His statement: ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾. The discussion of its i'rab (grammatical analysis) and its meaning has already preceded in the surah before this one, so we do not repeat it.

Likewise, the discussion of the meaning of ﴿tanzīl﴾ (revelation) and its i'rab has already preceded.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash said: ﴿Tanzīl﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿a Book whose verses are made clear﴾. Al-Farra' said: It is permissible that it be by supposing a hidden [predicate] of this, and it is also permissible to say that ﴿a Book﴾ is an appositive (badal) of ﴿tanzīl﴾, and ﴿from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is connected to ﴿tanzīl﴾.

The meaning of ﴿whose verses are made clear﴾ is: they are explained, or made into varied styles. Qatada said: They are made clear by explaining its lawful from its unlawful, and obedience from disobedience. Al-Hasan said: By promise and threat. Sufyan said: By reward and punishment. There is no barrier to applying it to all of these.

The clause is in the accusative position as a description (ṣifah) of ﴿a Book﴾. It was also read as ﴿fuṣilat﴾ with lightened pronunciation, meaning: it distinguished between truth and falsehood. The accusative of ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: its verses were made clear while it was an Arabic Qur'an.

Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative for praise. It was said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: he recites it as a Qur'an. It was said: it is a second object of ﴿fuṣilat﴾. It was said: it is by a hidden verb indicated by ﴿fuṣilat﴾, meaning: We made it clear as an Arabic Qur'an. ﴿For a people who know﴾ means: they know its meanings and understand them, and they are the people of the Arabic tongue.

Al-Dahhak said: meaning, they know that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah.

Mujahid said: meaning, they know that He is one God in the Torah and the Gospel. The lam is connected to a deleted element, as another description of ﴿Qur'an﴾, meaning: existing for a people; or it is connected to ﴿fuṣilat﴾. The first is preferable.

Likewise ﴿a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ are two other descriptions of ﴿Qur'an﴾, or two circumstantial states of ﴿a Book﴾. The meaning: a bringer of good tidings to the friends of Allah and a warner to His enemies.

It was also read as ﴿bashīrun wa-nadhīrun﴾ in the nominative, as descriptions of ﴿a Book﴾, or as predicates of a deleted subject.

﴿But most of them turned away﴾: by "most" here is meant the disbelievers, meaning: the disbelievers turned away from what it contained of warning. ﴿So they do not hear﴾: a hearing by which they benefit, because of their turning away from it.

﴿And they say: our hearts are in coverings﴾: meaning, in wrappings like a quiver in which arrows are kept, so it does not understand what you say, and your speech does not reach it. The word ﴿akinna﴾ is the plural of ﴿kinān﴾, which is a covering. Mujahid said: the kinān for the heart is like the shield for the arrow. The explanation of this has already preceded in al-Baqarah. ﴿And in our ears is a heaviness﴾: meaning deafness; the root of waqr is heaviness.

Talha ibn Musarrif read ﴿wiqr﴾ with a kasrah on the waw, and it was also read with a fatḥah on the waw and the qaf. The ﴿min﴾ in ﴿and between us and between you there is a barrier﴾ is for the beginning of the limit. The meaning: the barrier began from us and began from you, so the intermediate space between our direction and your direction is filled with the barrier, with no empty gap in it. These are images of the dullness of their hearts in grasping the truth, the rejection of their ears for it, and the impossibility of connection between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾: meaning, act according to your religion, indeed we act according to our religion.

Al-Kalbi said: act for our destruction, for indeed we act for your destruction. Muqatil said: act for your God who sent you, for indeed we act for our gods that we worship. It was said: act for your Hereafter, for indeed we act for our worldly life.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to answer their statement, and He said: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me that your God is one God﴾. Meaning: I am only like one of you, were it not for the revelation, and I am not of a different kind from you, such that your hearts would be in coverings from what I call you to, and in your ears a heaviness, and between me and you a barrier. I have not called you to what opposes reason; rather, I call you to monotheism. The majority read ﴿yūḥā﴾ in the passive. Al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i read it in the active, meaning: Allah reveals to me.

It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: I am not able to compel you to faith by force. I am a human being like you, and I have no distinction over you except that monotheism and the command to it are revealed to me. So upon me is only the delivery; if you accept, you will be guided, and if you refuse, you will be destroyed.

It was also said: the meaning is: I am not an angel; I am only a human being like you, and it has been revealed to me apart from you. So by revelation I became a prophet, and it became obligatory upon you to follow me.

Al-Hasan said concerning the meaning of the verse: Allah, glory be to Him, taught His Messenger (ﷺ) how to be humble.

﴿So go straight to Him﴾: it is transitive with ﴿ilā﴾ because it includes the meaning of "turn towards." The meaning: direct your uprightness to Him by obedience, do not incline away from His path, and seek His forgiveness for the sins that have passed from you.

Then He threatened and warned the polytheists, and said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾.

Then He described them by His statement: ﴿Who do not give zakāh﴾: meaning they withhold it and do not bring it out to the poor.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: they do not acknowledge its obligation.

Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: they do not give charity and do not spend in obedience.

It was said: the meaning of the verse is: they do not testify that there is no god but Allah, because that is the zakāh (purification) of souls and their cleansing.

Al-Farra' said: the polytheists used to spend expenses, give drink to the pilgrims and feed them, so they forbade that to whoever believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed concerning them.

﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿do not give﴾ and is included with it within the scope of the relative clause, meaning: they deny the Hereafter and reject it. The bringing of the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) is for the purpose of restriction.

﴿Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is a reward never cut off﴾: meaning, not cut off from them. It is said: "I cut the rope" (mannantu al-ḥabl) when you severed it. From this is the statement of al-Asbagh al-Azdi:

"By your life, I do not refuse, with a single bond, to a friend, nor is my goodness cut off."

It was also said: al-mamnūn means the diminished. Qutrub said this, and he recited the statement of Zuhayr:

"The superiority of the swift over the slow horses, so he does not give with it anything diminished or hasty."

Al-Jawhari said: al-mann is cutting, and it is said to mean reduction, and from it is the statement of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿for them is a reward never diminished﴾. Labid said:

"Dun-coloured, sharp-clawed, its food is not cut off."

Mujahid said: ﴿never cut off﴾ means: not counted. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: it is not bestowed upon them as a favour, because a favour is bestowed as grace, but as for the reward, its payment is a due right.

Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the sick, the disabled and the elderly, that when they become too weak for obedience, there is recorded for them the reward of what they used to do when they were in their best health.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to rebuke and reprimand them, and He said: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days?﴾ Meaning: do you disbelieve in the One whose matter is this great matter and whose power is this overwhelming power?

It was said: the two days are Sunday and Monday. It was said: what is meant is the measure of two days, because the true day only comes into being after the existence of the earth and the heaven.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿a-innakum﴾ with two hamzahs, the second between-between (bayna bayna, an intermediate sound). Ibn Kathir read it with one hamzah followed by a light yā'.

﴿And you set up rivals to Him﴾: meaning, equals and partners. The clause is conjoined to ﴿you disbelieve﴾ and falls under the interrogation. The reference with His statement ﴿that﴾ to the relative pronoun characterised by what has been mentioned is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. And among the worlds is what you set up as rivals to Allah. So how do you make some of His creatures partners with Him in worship?

His statement: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains﴾ is conjoined to ﴿created﴾, meaning: how do you disbelieve in the One who created the earth and placed in it firm mountains, meaning: firm mountains above it. It was said: the clause ﴿and He placed in it firm mountains﴾ is a new sentence, not conjoined to ﴿created﴾, because the separation between them is by something foreign.

The first is preferable, because the separating clause confirms the content of what came before it, so it has the status of emphasis. The meaning of ﴿above it﴾ is that they are elevated over it, because they are parts of the earth, and they differ from it only in respect of elevation, so in this respect they are as though distinct from it.

﴿And He blessed in it﴾: meaning He made it blessed, abundant in good, by what He created in it of benefits for the servants.

Al-Suddi said: He made its trees grow. ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾. Qatada and Mujahid said: He created in it its rivers, its trees and its animals. Al-Hasan, Ikrima and al-Dahhak said: He measured in it the provisions of its people and what suits their livelihoods, from trades, trees and benefits. He placed in each land what He did not place in the other, so that some of them might live from others through trade and travel from one land to another. The meaning of ﴿in four days﴾: meaning, in completion of four days together with the two days preceding. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others.

Ibn al-Anbari said: an example of this is the statement of a speaker: "I went from Basra to Baghdad in ten days, and to Kufa in fifteen days," meaning: in completion of fifteen days. So the meaning is that the occurrence of all that preceded, from the creation of the earth and what follows it, was in four days.

The accusative of *sawaan* (سَواءً) is an emphatic infinitive (*maşdar mu'akkid*, an emphasizing verbal noun) for an omitted verb. It is an adjective describing "days," meaning: they became equal (*istawat sawaan*), in the sense of *istiwa'an* (equally, evenly). It may also be in the accusative of circumstance (*hal*) relating to "the earth" or to the pronouns referring to it.

Ibn Kathir's reading... (omitted)

The majority of readers recited *sawaan* in the accusative. Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Ya'qub and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd recited it in the genitive, making it an adjective of *ayyam* (days). Abu Ja'far recited it in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "in four days, complete and equal," and the phrase *lil-sa'ilin* (لِلسَّائِلِينَ, "for those who ask") is connected to *sawaan*, meaning "equal for those who ask." Or it is connected to an omitted element, as if it were said: "This restriction is for those who ask, 'How long was the earth and what is in it created?'" Or it is connected to *qaddara* (قَدَّرَ, "He measured"), meaning: He measured in it its sustenance for the seekers who are in need of it.

Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the sentence, and the meaning is: "He measured in it its sustenance, equal for those in need, in four days." Ibn Jarir chose this view.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the creation of the earth and what is in it, He mentioned the manner of His creating the heavens. So He said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, meaning He purposed and directed Himself toward it with a straight intention.

Al-Razi said: it is from their saying *istawa ila makan kadha* ("he went straight to such a place") when one directs oneself to it in such a way that he does not turn toward any other task. It is from *al-istiwa'* (straightness), which is the opposite of crookedness. Its parallel is their saying *istaqama ilayhi* ("he proceeded straight toward it"), and from it the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So go straight to Him﴾. The meaning is: then the caller of wisdom called Him to create the heavens after creating the earth and what is in it.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is that His command ascended to the heaven while it was smoke. *Al-dukhan* (الدُّخانُ, "smoke") is what rises from the flame of fire, and it is used metaphorically for what is seen as vapor from the earth.

The exegetes said: this smoke is the vapor of water. Allah, exalted is He, specified the *istiwa'* toward the heaven, although the address that follows is directed to both it and the earth, as His saying indicates: ﴿He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly."﴾ This is done with reliance on what was previously mentioned of their measuring and the measuring of what is in them. The meaning of *i'tiya* (ائْتِيا, "come") is: do what I command you and come with it, just as one says *i'ti ma huwa al-ahsan* ("bring what is best"), meaning: do it.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said that Allah, exalted is He, said: "As for you, O heaven, bring forth your sun, your moon and your stars. As for you, O earth, split your rivers, bring forth your fruits and your plants."

The majority recited ﴿ائْتِيا﴾ as an imperative from *al-ityan* (coming). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid recited *atiya qalata atayna* with a long vowel (madd) in both places. It is either from *al-mu'atah* (مُؤَاتَاةِ), which is agreement, meaning that each of you should agree with the other, or from *al-iyta'* (الإيتاءِ), which is giving. Its pattern according to the first is *fa'ila* like *qatila*, and according to the second *af'ila* like *akrima*. ﴿Willingly or unwillingly﴾: both are verbal nouns in the position of circumstance, meaning obedient or compelled. Al-A'mash recited *kurhan* with a *damma*.

Al-Zajjaj said: obey obediently, or be compelled into compliance.

It was said: the meaning of this command to them is subjugation, that is: be, and they were, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl 16:40]. The speech is therefore a figure of speech demonstrating the effect of His power and the impossibility of their refusal. ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾ meaning: we come to your command submissively. He combined them in the plural of the rational, because He addressed them with what is addressed to rational beings.

Al-Qurtubi said: most scholars said that Allah, exalted is He, created speech in them, so they spoke as He willed, exalted is He. It was also said that this is an illustration of the manifestation of obedience from them and the effect of the Lordly power upon them.

﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾, meaning He created them, perfected them and finished with them, as in the verse of the poet:

*And upon them two coats of mail, which Dawud completed,*
*or which the maker of the flowing coats, Tubba', made.*

The pronoun in *qada-hunna* (قَضاهُنَّ) either refers to the heaven according to its meaning, since it is seven heavens, or it is an ambiguous pronoun explained by *seven heavens*. The accusative of *sab'a samawat* is either an explanation (*tafsir*) or a substitution (*badal*) of the pronoun.

It was said that its accusative is as the second object of *qada-hunna*, because it is implicitly meaning "making them." It was said it is an accusative of circumstance, meaning: He completed them while they were numbered as seven. Then *qada* means *sana'a* (made). It was also said that it is an accusative of specification (*tamyiz*). The meaning of *fi yawmayn* (في يَوْمَيْنِ, "in two days") is as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾, so the total is six days, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-A'raf 7:3]. Its explanation was previously given in Surat al-A'raf.

Mujahid said: one day of the six days is like a thousand years of what you count.

'Abd Allah ibn Salam said: He created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and measured in it its sustenance on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens on Thursday and Friday.

His saying ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾ is conjoined to *qada-hunna*.

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: meaning He created in it its sun, its moon, its stars, its orbits, and what is in them of angels, seas, hail and snow.

It was said: the meaning is that He inspired in them what He willed and what He commanded. Revelation (*al-iha'*) may also mean command, as in His saying: ﴿That your Lord has revealed to it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:5], and His saying: ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:111], meaning: I commanded them.

The combination of this verse with His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:30] has been considered problematic, since what is in this verse, "Then He turned to the heaven," indicates that its creation was later than the creation of the earth, and its apparent meaning contradicts His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾. It was said that the *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") in ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ is not for temporal sequence but for sequence of rank (*rutbi*), and the problem is thus resolved from its root. Even if it is for temporal sequence, the combination is possible: the creation of the earth precedes the creation of the heaven, and its spreading (*dahw*), meaning its extension, is an additional matter beyond the mere creation of it. So it is previously created but later spread out. This is apparent. Perhaps further clarification of the matter will come when we explain His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾, God willing.

﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾, meaning with shining, glittering stars upon it, like the glitter of lamps. The accusative of *hifzan* (حِفْظًا, "as protection") is either a verbal noun emphasizing an omitted verb, meaning: and We protected them with protection, or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), on the assumption: and We created the lamps as adornment and protection. The first is preferable.

Abu Hayyan said: the second view is a strain and a departure from what is simple and clear. The protection meant is protecting the heaven from the devils who steal hearing. The reference in His saying *dhalika* (ذَلِكَ, "that") is to what has been mentioned. ﴿The decree of the Mighty, the Knowing﴾, meaning the one most capable and most knowing.

﴿But if they turn away﴾ from reflection and contemplation upon these creatures, ﴿then say: "I have warned you"﴾, meaning: then say to them, O Muhammad, "I have warned you, I have frightened you, ﴿of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾," meaning a punishment like their punishment. The intended meaning of *al-sa'iqa* (الصَّاعِقَةُ, "thunderbolt") is destructive punishment of every kind.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-sa'iqa* is the destroying blow, whatever it may be.

The majority recited *sa'iqatan* (صاعِقَةً) in both places with an *alif*. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Nakha'i, al-Sulami and Ibn Muhaysin recited *sa'qatan* (صَعْقَةً) in both places. The meaning of *al-sa'iqa* and *al-sa'qa* was previously explained in al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿when the messengers came to them﴾ is a temporal clause (*zarf*) modifying either ﴿I have warned you﴾ or *sa'iqatan*, because it means punishment. That is: "I have warned you of the punishment that fell at the time when the messengers came." Or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the thunderbolt of 'Ad.

This is preferable to the first two views, because the warning did not occur at the time the messengers came, so it cannot correctly be a temporal clause for it. Likewise, the thunderbolt cannot correctly have that time as its temporal clause.

His saying ﴿from before them and from behind them﴾ is connected to *jaa'at-hum* (came to them), meaning: they came to them from all their sides. It was also said the meaning is: the messengers who came before and after came to them, by treating the arrival of their speech as the arrival of themselves, as if the messengers had come to them and addressed them with their saying: ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾, meaning: that you not worship. *Anna* here is the verbal (*masdariyya*) particle. It may also be the explanatory (*tafsiriyya*) particle, or the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, whose noun is an omitted pronoun of matter (*dhamir sha'n*).

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned their reply to the messengers, and said: ﴿They said: "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels"﴾, meaning: He would have sent them to us, and He did not send to us a human being of our kind.

Then they openly declared disbelief without hesitation, and said: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾, meaning: we disbelieve in what you claim, that Allah sent you to us, because you are human beings like us with no superiority over us. So how did He single you out with His message rather than us? The reply to this feeble doubt, which they raised, has already been given in more than one place.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat﴾ that he said: they do not testify that there is no god but Allah. And concerning His saying: ﴿For them is a reward never to be cut off﴾, he said: never to be diminished.

Ibn Jarir and al-Nahhas in his *Nasikh*, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from him that: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about the creation of the heavens and the earth. He said: Allah created the earth on Sunday and Monday, created the mountains and what is in them of benefits on Tuesday, and on Wednesday He created trees, stone, water, cities, civilization and ruin. These are four days. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: 'Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and you set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds.' He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask﴾. And He created the heaven on Thursday, and created on Friday the stars, the sun, the moon and the angels, until three hours remained of it. In the first of these three hours He created the terms of life, when each one who dies dies. In the second He cast into it everything of benefit. In the third He created Adam, settled him in the Garden, commanded Iblis to prostrate to him, and expelled him from it in the last hour." The Jews said: "Then what, O Muhammad?" He said: "Then He established Himself upon the Throne." They said: "You have been right, had you completed it." They said: "Then He rested." The Prophet (ﷺ) became very angry, and then there was revealed: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Qaf 50:38–39].

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, concerning His saying ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾, that he said: He split the rivers, planted the trees, set the mountains, made the seas flow, and placed in this what is not in that, and in that what is not in this.

Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him, saying: Allah, exalted is He, created a day and named it Sunday, then created a second and named it Monday, then created a third and named it Tuesday, then created a fourth and named it Wednesday, then created a fifth and named it Thursday, and he mentioned something similar to what was previously mentioned.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah finished His creation in six days," and he mentioned something similar to what was previously mentioned.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Bakr something similar to what was previously narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ that he said: He said to the heaven: "Bring forth your sun, your moon and your stars," and to the earth: "Split your rivers and bring forth your fruits." ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying *i'tiya* (ائْتِيا): he said, "Give." And concerning His saying *ataina* (أتَيْنا): he said, "We gave."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verse 15–24 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, had mentioned 'Ad and Thamud in summary, He mentioned, in detail, what belongs to each of the two groups. He said: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right﴾. That is: they were too proud to believe in Allah and to accept His messengers, and they exalted themselves over the people of the earth without right, meaning without any entitlement to that pride and tyranny which they displayed.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned some of the statements that came from them, which indicate their arrogance. He said: ﴿And they said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?"﴾ They were people of tall bodies and great strength, so they were deceived by their bodies when Hud threatened them with punishment. What they meant by this statement was that they were able to repel the punishment that would descend upon them. Allah responded to them with His words: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach: did they not know that Allah is mightier than them in power, and that He is able to send down upon them whatever kinds of His punishment He wills, by His saying "Be," and it is?

﴿And they had been rejecting Our signs﴾. That is: Our miracles which Allah gave to the messengers and made a proof of their prophethood, or Our signs which We sent down to Our messengers, or Our cosmic signs which We set up for them and made a proof against them, or all of that.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what He sent down upon them of His punishment. He said: ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind (ريح صرصر, rīḥ ṣarṣar)﴾. Ṣarṣar: the strong wind loud of sound, from ṣirra, which is a cry.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of ṣarṣar is "severe and violent." Al-Farra' said: it is the cold, which burns as fire burns.

'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada said: it is the cold. Qutrub recited the verse of al-Hutay'a:

"The feeders when a ṣarṣara blows, and the bearers when they are asked for the blood-money by people"

That is: when they are asked for the diya (blood-money).

Mujahid said: it is the one of intense poison-wind (samum). The more apt interpretation is cold, because ṣirr in the speech of the Arabs means cold, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"For it are pools like the horns of women, set in a day of wind and ṣirr"

Ibn al-Sikkit said: ṣarṣar may be from ṣirr, which is cold, and it may be from ṣarṣara al-bab (to slam the door) and from ṣarra, which is a cry; and from it is ﴿Then his wife came forward in a cry﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 29].

Then He, glory be to Him, specified the time of the descent of that punishment upon them. He said: ﴿On days of ill omen (nahisat)﴾. That is: inauspicious, bringing misfortune.

Mujahid and Qatada said: they were from the last Wednesday of Shawwal to the next Wednesday, which is seven nights and eight days, "in succession." It was said: nahisat means cold; it was said: consecutive; it was said: severe; it was said: full of dust.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "nahsat" with the ḥā' sukūn, as the plural of nahs. The rest read it with kasra. Abu Hatim preferred the first reading because of His saying: ﴿On a day of continuous misfortune﴾ [al-Qamar: 19]. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the second reading: ﴿That We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾, that is, so that We might make them taste it. Khizy is humiliation and abasement because of that arrogance. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing﴾, that is, more severe in humiliation and abasement. Describing the punishment with this is, in reality, a description of those punished, because they are the ones who became characterized by disgrace. ﴿And they will not be helped﴾, that is: they will not be prevented from the punishment descending upon them, and no one will repel it from them.

Then He mentioned the state of the other group, saying: ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾, that is: We made clear to them the path of salvation and guided them to the way of truth by sending messengers to them and setting up for them signs from Allah's creation, for these necessitate that every intelligent person believe in Allah and accept His messengers.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning of the verse is: We guided them to the path of good by sending messengers.

The majority read ﴿Thamud﴾ in the nominative with no tanwin (ghayr munsarif). Al-A'mash and Ibn Waththab read it in the nominative with tanwin. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Asim in one narration read it in the accusative with tanwin. Al-Hasan, Ibn Hurmuz and 'Asim in one narration read it in the accusative without tanwin. As for the nominative, it is by way of inception (ibtida'), and the clause following it is the predicate. As for the accusative, it is by way of occupation (ishtighal). As for the tanwin, it is by interpreting the name as a father or a tribe (al-hayy). As for the absence of tanwin, it is by interpreting it as the tribe (al-qabila).

﴿So they preferred blindness over guidance﴾, that is: they chose disbelief over faith. Abu al-'Aliya said: they chose blindness over clarity. As-Suddi said: they chose disobedience over obedience.

﴿So the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them﴾. It has already been mentioned that ṣā'iqa (thunderbolt) is a name for whatever destroys, regardless of what it is, and al-hūn is humiliation and abasement. So it is as if He said: the destroying punishment of humiliation or abasement struck them. It is said: "a humiliating punishment" (ʿadhāb hūn), meaning "humiliating" (muhin), like His saying: ﴿They remained in the humiliating punishment﴾ [Saba': 14]. The ba' in ﴿because of what they used to earn﴾ indicates causation, that is: because of what they used to earn, or because of their earning.

﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah﴾. They were Salih and those with him among the believers, for Allah saved them from that punishment.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned what He punished them with in this world, He mentioned what He punished them with in the Hereafter.
