Mujahid and ʿIkrimah said: they remained steadfast upon the testimony that there is no god but God until they died. Al-Thawri said: they acted in accordance with what they said. Al-Rabiʿ said: they turned away from everything other than God. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: they renounced the transient world and desired the everlasting one.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾ from God, glory be to Him, with the glad tidings they desire, whether bringing benefit, averting harm, or removing sorrow.

Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: they descend upon them at death. Muqatil and Qatadah said: when they rise from their graves for resurrection. Waki' said: the glad tidings come in three places: at death, in the grave, and at resurrection. ﴿That do not fear and do not grieve﴾: the *an* here is either the light (*mukhaffafah*) form, or the explanatory (*mufassirah*), or the governing (*nasibah*) form. ﻿*Lā* on the first two views is prohibitive, and on the third it is negative. The meaning is: do not fear what you are about to face of the affairs of the Hereafter, and do not grieve over what has escaped you of the affairs of this world, of family, children and wealth.

Mujahid said: do not fear death, and do not grieve over your children, for God is your successor over them. ʿAta' said: do not fear the rejection of your reward, for it is accepted; and do not grieve over your sins, for I forgive them for you.

The apparent view is that the descent of the angels upon them is not restricted to a specific time, and that the negation of fear and grief is not restricted to a particular state, as the omission of the complement in all of these indicates. ﴿And rejoice in the Paradise which you were promised﴾ in this world, for you will surely reach it, settle in it, and remain eternal in its bliss.

Then He, glory be to Him, gave them glad tidings of something greater than all that, saying: ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾: that is, We are those who take charge of your protection and support in the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter. Whoever God takes as his ally succeeds in every aim and is saved from every fear. It was said: this is the speech of the angels. Mujahid said: they say to them, "We are your companions who were with you in this world; when the Day of Resurrection comes, we will not leave you until you enter Paradise." Al-Suddi said: "We are the guardians of your deeds in this world and your allies in the Hereafter." It was said: they will intercede for them in the Hereafter and receive them with honour.

﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ of all kinds of pleasures and varieties of blessings. ﴿And for you therein is whatever you ask for﴾: that is, whatever you wish for. It is a form of *iftiʿal* (the reflexive form) from *duʿa'* (calling, supplication) in the sense of *talab* (request). The explanation of this meaning has already been given fully in His words: ﴿And for them is what they ask for﴾ [Yasin 36:57]. The difference between the two clauses is that the first is in terms of the desires of their souls, while the second is in terms of what they request, which is more general, so that it may include what their souls desire and what they do not.

Al-Razi said: in my view the closer possibility is that His words ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ refer to the spiritual Paradise mentioned in His words: ﴿Their call therein will be: Glory be to You, O God﴾ [Yunus 10:10], and so on.

The accusative of ﴿as hospitality from the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is either a circumstantial qualifier of the relative pronoun, or of its returning pronoun, or of the subject of *tadʿūn* (you ask for), or it is a verbal noun emphasizing an omitted verb, meaning: We sent it down as hospitality. *Nuzul* (hospitality) is what is prepared for them upon their arrival, of provision and entertainment, and its verification has already been discussed in Surah Al ʿImran.

﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God﴾: that is, to the oneness of God and His obedience. Al-Hasan said: he is the believer who answered God's call and called people to what God had enjoined on them of His obedience [p. 1316] in which God answered him; ﴿and acts righteously﴾ in response; ﴿and says: Indeed I am of the Muslims﴾ before my Lord.

Ibn Sirin, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: he is the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him). This is also narrated from al-Hasan.

ʿIkrimah, Qays ibn Abi Hazim and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the *muʾadhdhinun* (those who call to prayer). This is answered by saying that the verse is Meccan, while the adhan was legislated in Medina.

The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality, as the wording requires, and it includes first and foremost whoever was the cause of its revelation. So everyone who combined calling the servants to what God has legislated with doing righteous deeds, which means performing what God has obligated upon him while avoiding what He has forbidden to him, and who was among the Muslims in religion and not others, then there is nothing better than him, nor clearer than his way, nor greater in reward than his deed.

Then He, glory be to Him, explained the difference between good deeds and their evils, saying: ﴿And good and evil are not equal﴾: that is, the good deed with which God is pleased and for which He rewards is not equal to the evil deed which God dislikes and for which He punishes. There is no basis for restricting the good deed to a particular kind of acts of obedience, or the evil deed to a particular kind of acts of disobedience, for the wording is wider than that. It was said: the good deed is *tawhid* and the evil deed is shirk. It was said: the good deed is patient tolerance and the evil deed is harshness. It was said: the good deed is pardon and the evil deed is retaliation. It was said: the good deed is knowledge and the evil deed is obscenity.

Al-Farra' said: the *lā* in His words ﴿nor is the evil﴾ is superfluous.

﴿Repel with that which is better﴾: that is, repel the evil when it comes to you from the evildoer with the best good deed by which it can be repelled, and from this is repaying evil with good, and wrongdoing with pardon, anger with patience, overlooking slips, and bearing with what is disliked.

Mujahid and ʿAta' said: "with that which is better" means with greeting when meeting one who is hostile, and it was said: with a handshake at the time of meeting. ﴿Then the one between whom and you there is enmity [will become] as if he were a devoted friend﴾. This is the benefit resulting from repelling with that which is better. The meaning is: when you do that repelling, the enemy becomes like a friend, and the distant one becomes like the near one.

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who was hostile to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and then became his ally through the marriage that took place between them; then he embraced Islam and became a devoted ally in Islam through that marriage. It was also said other than this. The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality.

﴿But none is granted it except those who are patient﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: none receives this act and this state, which is repelling evil with good, except those who are patient in restraining anger and enduring what is disliked. ﴿But none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ in reward and goodness.

Qatadah said: "The great fortune (al-hazz al-'azim) in Paradise," meaning: "None is granted it (yulaqqaha) except those for whom Paradise is decreed." It was also said that the pronoun in *yulaqqaha* refers to Paradise, and it was said that it refers to the word of Tawhid (the declaration of God's oneness).

The majority of reciters read *yulaqqaha* from *al-talqiyah* (to be granted or made to receive). Talhah ibn Musarrif and Ibn Kathir, in one narration from him, read *yulaqqaha* (يُلاقاها) from *al-mula>qah* (to meet or encounter).

Then, glorified is He, commanded him to seek refuge in God from Satan, saying: ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should incite you, then seek refuge in God﴾. *Al-nazgh* (an evil prompting) resembles a prod (*al-nakhs*), and the whispering (*al-waswasah*) is likened to it because it urges toward evil. The meaning is: if Satan turns you away from something that God has prescribed for you, or from repelling evil with that which is better, then seek refuge in God from his evil. The *nazgh* is described as the one doing the inciting by way of *al-majaz al-'aqli* (figurative attribution in the rational sense, i.e., ascribing an act to something other than its real agent), as in their saying: "the grandfather of his grandfather." The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it, meaning: All-Hearing of everything that is heard, and All-Knowing of everything that is known. Whoever is like this grants refuge to whoever seeks refuge in Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ), while he was in Makkah, would raise his voice when reciting the Qur'an. The polytheists would drive people away from him, saying: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and talk noisily during it, that perhaps you may overcome﴾. And when he lowered his recitation, he would not be heard by anyone who wished to hear the Qur'an. So God revealed: ﴿Do not be loud in your prayer, nor be silent therein﴾ [al-Isra' 110]."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he was asked about the words: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who led us astray, among the jinn and mankind﴾, and he said: "It is the son of Adam who killed his brother, and Iblis."

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited to us this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who say, 'Our Lord is God,' and then remain steadfast﴾, and said: 'Some people have said it, then most of them disbelieved. Whoever says it when he is dying, he is among those who remained steadfast in it.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak, 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Musaddad, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, through the chain of Sa'id ibn 'Imran, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾, that he said: "Steadfastness is that they do not associate anything with God."

Ibn Rahawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated, through the chain of al-Aswad ibn Hilal, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that he said: "What do you say about these two verses: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾, and ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾?" They said: "Those who say, 'Our Lord is God,' then act upon it and remain steadfast upon His command, without sinning, and who do not mix their belief with wrongdoing, meaning they do not sin." He said: "You have carried both of them to a difficult matter. ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ means with shirk (associating partners with God), and ﴿those who say, "Our Lord is God," then remain steadfast﴾ means they did not return to the worship of idols."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from some of the Companions: "Then they remained steadfast upon the obligations of God."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿then remained steadfast﴾ that he said: "Upon the testimony that there is no god but God."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," then remain steadfast﴾ that he said: "They remained steadfast in obedience to God and did not swerve, swerving like a fox."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Darimi, al-Bukhari in his History, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Hibban narrated from Sufyan al-Thaqafi that "a man said: 'O Messenger of God, tell me a matter in Islam about which I will not need to ask anyone after you.' He said: 'Say: I have believed in God, then be steadfast.' I said: 'What should I guard against?' So he pointed to his tongue." al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan sahih."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah concerning His words: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God﴾, she said: "The muezzin (caller to prayer)." ﴿And does righteous deeds﴾, she said: "Two rak'ahs between the adhan and the iqamah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from another route from her, who said: "I do not think this verse was revealed except concerning the muezzins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿The good and the evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾, that he said: "He commanded the Muslims to be patient when angry, to be forbearing when ignorant, and to pardon when wronged. When they do that, God protects them from Satan, and their enemy submits to them, ﴿as if he were a devoted friend﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾, that he said: "Greet him with peace, and then the one between you and him who is hostile will be as if he were a devoted friend."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas concerning His words: ﴿And none is granted it except those who are patient﴾, that he said: "A man is insulted by his brother, and he says: 'If you are truthful, may God forgive me, and if you are lying, may God forgive you.'"

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sulayman ibn Surad, who said: "Two men abused each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the anger of one of them intensified. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, I know a word which, if he said it, the anger would leave him: I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed.' The man said: 'Am I mad, that you see me so?' Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should incite you, then seek refuge in God. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾."

(p-1317)

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verses 25–36 (part 1 of 2)**

His words, ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾: that is, We prepared for them companions from among the devils.

Al-Zajjaj said: We caused them to have companions until they led them astray. It was also said: We empowered companions over them. It was also said: We decreed them. The meanings are close. The root of *taqyid* (appointing) is facilitation and arrangement. The *quranaʾ* (companions) is the plural of *qarin* (companion), and they are the devils. He made them like close friends to them.

It was said that God appointed for them companions in the Fire. The more preferable view is that this is in this world, because of His words: ﴿and they made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them﴾. The meaning is: they made attractive to them what was before them of the affairs of this world and its desires, and they drove them to fall into the disobedience of God by their immersion in it. And they made attractive to them what was behind them of the affairs of the Hereafter, so they said: there is no resurrection, no reckoning, no Paradise and no Fire.

Al-Zajjaj said: "What is before them" is what they have done, and "what is behind them" is what they have resolved to do.

It is also narrated from al-Zajjaj that he said: "What is before them" is the matter of the Hereafter, namely that there is no resurrection, no Paradise and no Fire, and "what is behind them" is the matter of this world. ﴿And the word has come due against them﴾: that is, the punishment has become obligatory and firmly established against them. This is His words, glory be to Him: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you among them, all together﴾ [Sad 38:85]. ﴿Among nations﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ʿalayhim (against them). The meaning is: existing within a body of nations. It was said that *fi* here means *maʿa* (with), that is: with nations of the disbelieving nations which had passed and gone before them. ﴿From before them, of jinn and humankind﴾ in disbelief. The clause ﴿Indeed they were losers﴾ gives the reason for their deserving the punishment.

﴿And those who disbelieved said: Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾: that is, some of them said to others: Do not listen to it and do not give it attention. It was said: the meaning of "do not listen" is: do not obey. It is said: "I listened to you," meaning: "I obeyed you." ﴿And make noise during it﴾: that is, oppose it with idle talk and falsehood, or raise your voices so that the reciter is confused.

Mujahid said: "Make noise during it" means with whistling, clapping, hand-clapping, and mixing words together until it becomes idle talk. Al-Dahhak said: Speak a great deal so that what he says becomes confused for him. Abu al-Aliyah said: Find fault with it and defame it.

[p. 1315] The majority read ﴿wa-l-ghaw﴾ (and make noise) with a *fatha* on the *ghayn*, from *laghā* (he spoke idle talk) when he spoke with *laghw*, which is what has no benefit in it; or from *laghā* with *fatha* also, *yalghā* with *fatha* also, as al-Akhfash related. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi, Qatadah, al-Sammak and al-Zaʿfarani read it with a *damma* on the *ghayn*.

The discussion of *laghw* (idle talk) has already been mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. ﴿So that you may overcome﴾: that is, so that you may overcome them and they fall silent.

Then He, glory be to Him, threatened them for that, saying: ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment﴾. This is a threat to all the disbelievers, and those with whom the context is concerned enter into it first. ﴿And We will surely recompense them for the worst of what they used to do﴾: that is, We will surely recompense them in the Hereafter for the worst of their deeds which they did in this world. Muqatil said: that is shirk (associating partners with God). It was said: the meaning is that He recompenses them for the evils of their deeds and not for their good deeds, such as their kinship ties and their honouring of guests, because that is false and has no reward for them given their disbelief.

The indication in His words *dhalika* (that) refers to what was mentioned before. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿the recompense of the enemies of God is the Fire﴾; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter is that. The clause ﴿the recompense of the enemies of God is the Fire﴾ explains the clause before it. The first is preferable. "The Fire" may be an apposition to "the recompense," or a substitute for it, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or the subject with the predicate being ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity﴾.

On the three first possibilities, the clause ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ is a new sentence confirming what came before it. The meaning of "the abode of eternity" is: the abode of continuous residence which has no end. ﴿A recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾: that is, they are recompensed due to their denial of the signs of God.

Muqatil said: it means the Qur'an; they denied that it was from God. On this view, the expression of "denial" for "idle talk" is because it is its cause, establishing the cause in the position of the effect.

﴿And those who disbelieved said: Our Lord, show us those who led us astray from the jinn and humankind﴾. They said this while they were in the Fire, and He mentioned it in the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. The meaning is that they asked God, glory be to Him, to show them those who had led them astray from the groups of jinn and humankind, from among the devils who used to tempt them and drive them to acts of disobedience, and from among the leaders who used to make disbelief attractive to them.

It was said: the intended ones are Iblis and Qabil, because they initiated disobedience for the children of Adam.

The majority read *arina* (show us) with a *kasra* on the *rāʾ*. Ibn Muhaysin and al-Susi from Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read it with the *rāʾ* sukun, and Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal also read it so. They are two dialects with one meaning.

Al-Khalil said: if you say *arini thawbaka* with a *kasra*, its meaning is "make me see it," and with sukun it means "give it to me."

﴿We will place them beneath our feet﴾: that is, we will trample them with our feet so that we may be satisfied with them. It was said: we will make them lower than us in the Fire. ﴿So that they may be among the lowest﴾ in place within it, or among the most humiliated and degraded. It was said: so that they may suffer a worse punishment than us.

Then, when He had mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers and what He had prepared for them, He mentioned the state of the believers and the blessings He bestowed on them, saying: ﴿Indeed those who say: Our Lord is God﴾: that is, alone, with no partner for Him. ﴿Then remain steadfast﴾ upon *tawhid* (affirmation of God's oneness) and do not turn to any god other than God.

Al-Rabiʿ said: they turned away from everything other than God. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: they renounced the transient world and desired the everlasting one.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾ from God, glory be to Him, with the glad tidings they desire, whether bringing benefit, averting harm, or removing sorrow.

﴿Repel with that which is better﴾: that is, repel the evil when it comes to you from the evildoer with the best good deed by which it can be repelled, and from this is repaying evil with good, and wrongdoing with pardon, anger with patience, overlooking slips, and bearing with what is disliked.

Mujahid and ʿAta' said: "with that which is better" means with greeting when meeting one who is hostile, and it was said: with a handshake at the time of meeting. ﴿Then the one between whom and you there is enmity [will become] as if he were a devoted friend﴾. This is the benefit resulting from repelling with that which is better. The meaning is: when you do that repelling, the enemy becomes like a friend, and the distant one becomes like the near one.

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who was hostile to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and then became his ally through the marriage that took place between them; then he embraced Islam and became a devoted ally in Islam through that marriage. It was also said other than this. The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality.

﴿But none is granted it except those who are patient﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: none receives this act and this state, which is repelling evil with good, except those who are patient in restraining anger and enduring what is disliked. ﴿But none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ in reward and goodness.

Qatadah said: "The great fortune (al-hazz al-'azim) in Paradise," meaning: "None is granted it (yulaqqaha) except those for whom Paradise is decreed." It was also said that the pronoun in *yulaqqaha* refers to Paradise, and it was said that it refers to the word of Tawhid (the declaration of God's oneness).

The majority of reciters read *yulaqqaha* from *al-talqiyah* (to be granted or made to receive). Talhah ibn Musarrif and Ibn Kathir, in one narration from him, read *yulaqqaha* (يُلاقاها) from *al-mula>qah* (to meet or encounter).

Then, glorified is He, commanded him to seek refuge in God from Satan, saying: ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should incite you, then seek refuge in God﴾. *Al-nazgh* (an evil prompting) resembles a prod (*al-nakhs*), and the whispering (*al-waswasah*) is likened to it because it urges toward evil. The meaning is: if Satan turns you away from something that God has prescribed for you, or from repelling evil with that which is better, then seek refuge in God from his evil. The *nazgh* is described as the one doing the inciting by way of *al-majaz al-'aqli* (figurative attribution in the rational sense, i.e., ascribing an act to something other than its real agent), as in their saying: "the grandfather of his grandfather." The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it, meaning: All-Hearing of everything that is heard, and All-Knowing of everything that is known. Whoever is like this grants refuge to whoever seeks refuge in Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ), while he was in Makkah, would raise his voice when reciting the Qur'an. The polytheists would drive people away from him, saying: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and talk noisily during it, that perhaps you may overcome﴾. And when he lowered his recitation, he would not be heard by anyone who wished to hear the Qur'an. So God revealed: ﴿Do not be loud in your prayer, nor be silent therein﴾ [al-Isra' 110]."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he was asked about the words: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who led us astray, among the jinn and mankind﴾, and he said: "It is the son of Adam who killed his brother, and Iblis."

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited to us this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who say, 'Our Lord is God,' and then remain steadfast﴾, and said: 'Some people have said it, then most of them disbelieved. Whoever says it when he is dying, he is among those who remained steadfast in it.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak, 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Musaddad, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, through the chain of Sa'id ibn 'Imran, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾, that he said: "Steadfastness is that they do not associate anything with God."

Ibn Rahawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated, through the chain of al-Aswad ibn Hilal, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that he said: "What do you say about these two verses: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾, and ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾?" They said: "Those who say, 'Our Lord is God,' then act upon it and remain steadfast upon His command, without sinning, and who do not mix their belief with wrongdoing, meaning they do not sin." He said: "You have carried both of them to a difficult matter. ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ means with shirk (associating partners with God), and ﴿those who say, "Our Lord is God," then remain steadfast﴾ means they did not return to the worship of idols."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from some of the Companions: "Then they remained steadfast upon the obligations of God."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿then remained steadfast﴾ that he said: "Upon the testimony that there is no god but God."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," then remain steadfast﴾ that he said: "They remained steadfast in obedience to God and did not swerve, swerving like a fox."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Darimi, al-Bukhari in his History, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Hibban narrated from Sufyan al-Thaqafi that "a man said: 'O Messenger of God, tell me a matter in Islam about which I will not need to ask anyone after you.' He said: 'Say: I have believed in God, then be steadfast.' I said: 'What should I guard against?' So he pointed to his tongue." al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan sahih."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah concerning His words: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God﴾, she said: "The muezzin (caller to prayer)." ﴿And does righteous deeds﴾, she said: "Two rak'ahs between the adhan and the iqamah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from another route from her, who said: "I do not think this verse was revealed except concerning the muezzins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿The good and the evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾, that he said: "He commanded the Muslims to be patient when angry, to be forbearing when ignorant, and to pardon when wronged. When they do that, God protects them from Satan, and their enemy submits to them, ﴿as if he were a devoted friend﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾, that he said: "Greet him with peace, and then the one between you and him who is hostile will be as if he were a devoted friend."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas concerning His words: ﴿And none is granted it except those who are patient﴾, that he said: "A man is insulted by his brother, and he says: 'If you are truthful, may God forgive me, and if you are lying, may God forgive you.'"

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sulayman ibn Surad, who said: "Two men abused each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the anger of one of them intensified. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, I know a word which, if he said it, the anger would leave him: I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed.' The man said: 'Am I mad, that you see me so?' Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should incite you, then seek refuge in God. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verses 25–36 (part 1 of 2)**

His words, ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾: that is, We prepared for them companions from among the devils.

Al-Zajjaj said: We caused them to have companions until they led them astray. It was also said: We empowered companions over them. It was also said: We decreed them. The meanings are close. The root of *taqyid* (appointing) is facilitation and arrangement. The *quranaʾ* (companions) is the plural of *qarin* (companion), and they are the devils. He made them like close friends to them.

It was said that God appointed for them companions in the Fire. The more preferable view is that this is in this world, because of His words: ﴿and they made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them﴾. The meaning is: they made attractive to them what was before them of the affairs of this world and its desires, and they drove them to fall into the disobedience of God by their immersion in it. And they made attractive to them what was behind them of the affairs of the Hereafter, so they said: there is no resurrection, no reckoning, no Paradise and no Fire.

Al-Zajjaj said: "What is before them" is what they have done, and "what is behind them" is what they have resolved to do.

It is also narrated from al-Zajjaj that he said: "What is before them" is the matter of the Hereafter, namely that there is no resurrection, no Paradise and no Fire, and "what is behind them" is the matter of this world. ﴿And the word has come due against them﴾: that is, the punishment has become obligatory and firmly established against them. This is His words, glory be to Him: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you among them, all together﴾ [Sad 38:85]. ﴿Among nations﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ʿalayhim (against them). The meaning is: existing within a body of nations. It was said that *fi* here means *maʿa* (with), that is: with nations of the disbelieving nations which had passed and gone before them. ﴿From before them, of jinn and humankind﴾ in disbelief. The clause ﴿Indeed they were losers﴾ gives the reason for their deserving the punishment.

﴿And those who disbelieved said: Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾: that is, some of them said to others: Do not listen to it and do not give it attention. It was said: the meaning of "do not listen" is: do not obey. It is said: "I listened to you," meaning: "I obeyed you." ﴿And make noise during it﴾: that is, oppose it with idle talk and falsehood, or raise your voices so that the reciter is confused.

Mujahid said: "Make noise during it" means with whistling, clapping, hand-clapping, and mixing words together until it becomes idle talk. Al-Dahhak said: Speak a great deal so that what he says becomes confused for him. Abu al-Aliyah said: Find fault with it and defame it.

[p. 1315] The majority read ﴿wa-l-ghaw﴾ (and make noise) with a *fatha* on the *ghayn*, from *laghā* (he spoke idle talk) when he spoke with *laghw*, which is what has no benefit in it; or from *laghā* with *fatha* also, *yalghā* with *fatha* also, as al-Akhfash related. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi, Qatadah, al-Sammak and al-Zaʿfarani read it with a *damma* on the *ghayn*.

The discussion of *laghw* (idle talk) has already been mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. ﴿So that you may overcome﴾: that is, so that you may overcome them and they fall silent.

Then He, glory be to Him, threatened them for that, saying: ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment﴾. This is a threat to all the disbelievers, and those with whom the context is concerned enter into it first. ﴿And We will surely recompense them for the worst of what they used to do﴾: that is, We will surely recompense them in the Hereafter for the worst of their deeds which they did in this world. Muqatil said: that is shirk (associating partners with God). It was said: the meaning is that He recompenses them for the evils of their deeds and not for their good deeds, such as their kinship ties and their honouring of guests, because that is false and has no reward for them given their disbelief.

The indication in His words *dhalika* (that) refers to what was mentioned before. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿the recompense of the enemies of God is the Fire﴾; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter is that. The clause ﴿the recompense of the enemies of God is the Fire﴾ explains the clause before it. The first is preferable. "The Fire" may be an apposition to "the recompense," or a substitute for it, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or the subject with the predicate being ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity﴾.

On the three first possibilities, the clause ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ is a new sentence confirming what came before it. The meaning of "the abode of eternity" is: the abode of continuous residence which has no end. ﴿A recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs﴾: that is, they are recompensed due to their denial of the signs of God.

Muqatil said: it means the Qur'an; they denied that it was from God. On this view, the expression of "denial" for "idle talk" is because it is its cause, establishing the cause in the position of the effect.

﴿And those who disbelieved said: Our Lord, show us those who led us astray from the jinn and humankind﴾. They said this while they were in the Fire, and He mentioned it in the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. The meaning is that they asked God, glory be to Him, to show them those who had led them astray from the groups of jinn and humankind, from among the devils who used to tempt them and drive them to acts of disobedience, and from among the leaders who used to make disbelief attractive to them.

It was said: the intended ones are Iblis and Qabil, because they initiated disobedience for the children of Adam.

The majority read *arina* (show us) with a *kasra* on the *rāʾ*. Ibn Muhaysin and al-Susi from Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read it with the *rāʾ* sukun, and Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal also read it so. They are two dialects with one meaning.

Al-Khalil said: if you say *arini thawbaka* with a *kasra*, its meaning is "make me see it," and with sukun it means "give it to me."

﴿We will place them beneath our feet﴾: that is, we will trample them with our feet so that we may be satisfied with them. It was said: we will make them lower than us in the Fire. ﴿So that they may be among the lowest﴾ in place within it, or among the most humiliated and degraded. It was said: so that they may suffer a worse punishment than us.

Then, when He had mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers and what He had prepared for them, He mentioned the state of the believers and the blessings He bestowed on them, saying: ﴿Indeed those who say: Our Lord is God﴾: that is, alone, with no partner for Him. ﴿Then remain steadfast﴾ upon *tawhid* (affirmation of God's oneness) and do not turn to any god other than God.

A group of the Companions and the Successors said: the meaning of *istiqamah* (steadfastness) is sincerity of deed for God. Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "then remain steadfast" upon obedience to God. Al-Hasan said: they remained steadfast upon the command of God, so they acted in obedience to Him and avoided His disobedience. Mujahid and ʿIkrimah said: they remained steadfast upon the testimony that there is no god but God until they died. Al-Thawri said: they acted in accordance with what they said. Al-Rabiʿ said: they turned away from everything other than God. Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: they renounced the transient world and desired the everlasting one.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾ from God, glory be to Him, with the glad tidings they desire, whether bringing benefit, averting harm, or removing sorrow.

Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: they descend upon them at death. Muqatil and Qatadah said: when they rise from their graves for resurrection. Waki' said: the glad tidings come in three places: at death, in the grave, and at resurrection. ﴿That do not fear and do not grieve﴾: the *an* here is either the light (*mukhaffafah*) form, or the explanatory (*mufassirah*), or the governing (*nasibah*) form. ﻿*Lā* on the first two views is prohibitive, and on the third it is negative. The meaning is: do not fear what you are about to face of the affairs of the Hereafter, and do not grieve over what has escaped you of the affairs of this world, of family, children and wealth.

Mujahid said: do not fear death, and do not grieve over your children, for God is your successor over them. ʿAta' said: do not fear the rejection of your reward, for it is accepted; and do not grieve over your sins, for I forgive them for you.

The apparent view is that the descent of the angels upon them is not restricted to a specific time, and that the negation of fear and grief is not restricted to a particular state, as the omission of the complement in all of these indicates. ﴿And rejoice in the Paradise which you were promised﴾ in this world, for you will surely reach it, settle in it, and remain eternal in its bliss.

Then He, glory be to Him, gave them glad tidings of something greater than all that, saying: ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾: that is, We are those who take charge of your protection and support in the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter. Whoever God takes as his ally succeeds in every aim and is saved from every fear. It was said: this is the speech of the angels. Mujahid said: they say to them, "We are your companions who were with you in this world; when the Day of Resurrection comes, we will not leave you until you enter Paradise." Al-Suddi said: "We are the guardians of your deeds in this world and your allies in the Hereafter." It was said: they will intercede for them in the Hereafter and receive them with honour.

﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ of all kinds of pleasures and varieties of blessings. ﴿And for you therein is whatever you ask for﴾: that is, whatever you wish for. It is a form of *iftiʿal* (the reflexive form) from *duʿa'* (calling, supplication) in the sense of *talab* (request). The explanation of this meaning has already been given fully in His words: ﴿And for them is what they ask for﴾ [Yasin 36:57]. The difference between the two clauses is that the first is in terms of the desires of their souls, while the second is in terms of what they request, which is more general, so that it may include what their souls desire and what they do not.

Al-Razi said: in my view the closer possibility is that His words ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ refer to the spiritual Paradise mentioned in His words: ﴿Their call therein will be: Glory be to You, O God﴾ [Yunus 10:10], and so on.

The accusative of ﴿as hospitality from the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is either a circumstantial qualifier of the relative pronoun, or of its returning pronoun, or of the subject of *tadʿūn* (you ask for), or it is a verbal noun emphasizing an omitted verb, meaning: We sent it down as hospitality. *Nuzul* (hospitality) is what is prepared for them upon their arrival, of provision and entertainment, and its verification has already been discussed in Surah Al ʿImran.

﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God﴾: that is, to the oneness of God and His obedience. Al-Hasan said: he is the believer who answered God's call and called people to what God had enjoined on them of His obedience [p. 1316] in which God answered him; ﴿and acts righteously﴾ in response; ﴿and says: Indeed I am of the Muslims﴾ before my Lord.

Ibn Sirin, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: he is the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him). This is also narrated from al-Hasan.

ʿIkrimah, Qays ibn Abi Hazim and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the *muʾadhdhinun* (those who call to prayer). This is answered by saying that the verse is Meccan, while the adhan was legislated in Medina.

The preferable view is to take the verse in its generality, as the wording requires, and it includes first and foremost whoever was the cause of its revelation. So everyone who combined calling the servants to what God has legislated with doing righteous deeds, which means performing what God has obligated upon him while avoiding what He has forbidden to him, and who was among the Muslims in religion and not others, then there is nothing better than him, nor clearer than his way, nor greater in reward than his deed.

Then He, glory be to Him, explained the difference between good deeds and their evils, saying: ﴿And good and evil are not equal﴾: that is, the good deed with which God is pleased and for which He rewards is not equal to the evil deed which God dislikes and for which He punishes. There is no basis for restricting the good deed to a particular kind of acts of obedience, or the evil deed to a particular kind of acts of disobedience, for the wording is wider than that. It was said: the good deed is *tawhid* and the evil deed is shirk. It was said: the good deed is patient tolerance and the evil deed is harshness. It was said: the good deed is pardon and the evil deed is retaliation. It was said: the good deed is knowledge and the evil deed is obscenity.

Al-Farra' said: the *lā* in His words ﴿nor is the evil﴾ is superfluous.

﴿Repel with that which is better﴾: that is, repel the evil when it comes to you from the evildoer with the best good deed by which it can be repelled, and from this is repaying evil with good, and wrongdoing with pardon, anger with patience, overlooking slips, and bearing with what is disliked.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿then remained steadfast﴾ that he said: "Upon the testimony that there is no god but God."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," then remain steadfast﴾ that he said: "They remained steadfast in obedience to God and did not swerve, swerving like a fox."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Darimi, al-Bukhari in his History, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Hibban narrated from Sufyan al-Thaqafi that "a man said: 'O Messenger of God, tell me a matter in Islam about which I will not need to ask anyone after you.' He said: 'Say: I have believed in God, then be steadfast.' I said: 'What should I guard against?' So he pointed to his tongue." al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan sahih."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'ishah concerning His words: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God﴾, she said: "The muezzin (caller to prayer)." ﴿And does righteous deeds﴾, she said: "Two rak'ahs between the adhan and the iqamah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from another route from her, who said: "I do not think this verse was revealed except concerning the muezzins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿The good and the evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾, that he said: "He commanded the Muslims to be patient when angry, to be forbearing when ignorant, and to pardon when wronged. When they do that, God protects them from Satan, and their enemy submits to them, ﴿as if he were a devoted friend﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾, that he said: "Greet him with peace, and then the one between you and him who is hostile will be as if he were a devoted friend."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas concerning His words: ﴿And none is granted it except those who are patient﴾, that he said: "A man is insulted by his brother, and he says: 'If you are truthful, may God forgive me, and if you are lying, may God forgive you.'"

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sulayman ibn Surad, who said: "Two men abused each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the anger of one of them intensified. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, I know a word which, if he said it, the anger would leave him: I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed.' The man said: 'Am I mad, that you see me so?' Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should incite you, then seek refuge in God. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾."

(p-1317)

He, glory be to Him, began to explain some of His wondrous signs, which demonstrate His perfect power and the strength of His governance, in order to use them as evidence of His oneness. He said: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon.﴾ Then, having made clear that these are among His signs, He forbade them from worshipping the sun and the moon and commanded them to prostrate to God, mighty and majestic, saying: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon,﴾ because they are two of His created things, so it is not valid for them to be partners with Him in His lordship. ﴿But prostrate to God, who created them,﴾ meaning: who created these four things mentioned, since the plural of non-rational beings takes the rule of the plural of females, or of signs, or of the sun and the moon, because two is considered a plural according to a group of the imams. ﴿If it is Him you worship.﴾ It was said that some people used to prostrate to the sun and the moon, as the Sabians did in their worship of the stars, and they claimed that by prostrating to them they intended to prostrate to God, so they were forbidden from this. This is the reason for singling out prostration for the prohibition. It was also said that the reason for singling it out is that it is one of the highest levels of worship. This verse is, without disagreement, one of the verses of prostration, but they differed about its place. It was said that the place of prostration is at His saying: ﴿If it is Him you worship,﴾ because it is connected to the command. It was said that it is at His saying: ﴿and they do not tire,﴾ because it completes the speech.

﴿So if they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord glorify Him night and day, and they never tire.﴾ That is: if these people are arrogant towards compliance, then the angels continually glorify God, glory be to Him, night and day, and they never grow weary or slacken.

﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled.﴾ The address here is to everyone who is fit for it, or to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Khashi'a (humbled) means dry and barren.

It was said: it means the dusty ground that does not produce plants.

Al-Azhari said: when the earth dries out and does not receive rain, it is said: "it has become humbled." ﴿But when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells.﴾ That is, the water of rain. The meaning of "stirs" is that it moves with vegetation; it is said: "the man stirred" when he moved. From this is the saying of the poet:

"You see him like the blade of a sword, quivering for the dew, when you find with the evil man no food."

The meaning of "swells" is that it rises and increases before it grows, as Mujahid and others said. According to this, there is an inversion in the speech, and its order is: it swelled and stirred. It was also said: stirring and swelling may happen before the plant emerges and may happen after it. The linguistic meaning of rabw is elevation, as one says of a high place: rabwa and rabiya. The explanation of this verse was already given in full in Surah al-Hajj. It was also said: "stirred" means it rejoiced at the rain, and "swelled" means it swelled with plants.

Abu Ja'far and Khalid read: "warabat" (with a hamza).

﴿Indeed, He who revived it is the reviver of the dead,﴾ by resurrection and raising. ﴿Indeed, He is over all things competent.﴾ Nothing can overpower Him, whatever it may be.

﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs,﴾ that is, they incline away from the truth. Ilhad (deviation) is inclining and turning aside, and from it comes the lahd in the grave, because its side is inclined to one direction. It is said: "alhada fi dini Allah," meaning he inclined and turned away from it. It is also said: "lahada." The explanation of ilhad has already been given.

Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is that they incline away from belief in the Qur'an. Mujahid also said: they incline during the recitation of the Qur'an by whistling, clapping, idle talk, and singing. Qatada said: they lie concerning Our signs. Al-Suddi said: they oppose and contend.

Ibn Zayd said: they associate partners (with God). ﴿They are not hidden from Us;﴾ rather, We know them and will repay them for what they do.

Then He explained the manner of the recompense and the difference between the believer and the disbeliever, saying: ﴿Is he who is thrown into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ This interrogative is for affirmation, and its purpose is to alert that those who deviate concerning the signs will be thrown into the Fire, and that those who believe in them will come secure on the Day of Resurrection. (p-1318)

The apparent meaning of the verse is general, taking into account the generality of the wording and not the specific cause.

It was said: what is meant by "he who is thrown into the Fire" is Abu Jahl, and "he who comes secure" is the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: Hamza, and it was said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and it was said: Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi. ﴿Do what you will; indeed, He is seeing of what you do.﴾ This is an imperative of threat, meaning: do from your deeds, which will throw you into the Fire, whatever you wish. Indeed, He is seeing of what you do, so He will recompense you for everything you do.

Al-Zajjaj said: its wording is that of a command, but its meaning is a warning.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it came to them—﴾ This sentence is a new beginning confirming what came before it, and the predicate of inna is omitted. That is: indeed, those who disbelieved in the Qur'an when it came to them will be repaid for their disbelief, or they will perish, or they will be punished. It was said that it is His saying: ﴿They are called from a distant place,﴾ but this is far-fetched, even though Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' preferred it.

Al-Kisa'i said: the preceding predicate, which is ﴿they are not hidden from Us,﴾ takes its place.

It was also said that the sentence is a substitute (badal) for the first sentence, which is: "those who deviate concerning Our signs," and the predicate of inna is the earlier predicate. ﴿And indeed, it is a Book of might.﴾ That is, the Qur'an, concerning which they deviated; it is mighty, meaning it is protected from being opposed, and from being disparaged by those who disparage it, and it is secure from every defect.

Then He described it as being the truth, to which falsehood has no path in any way, saying: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it.﴾

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that it is protected from being diminished, so that falsehood would come to it from before it, or from being increased, so that falsehood would come to it from behind it. Qatada and al-Suddi also said this.

According to this, the meaning of falsehood is addition and subtraction.

Muqatil said: denial from the books that came before it cannot reach it, nor will any book come after it to nullify it. Al-Kalbi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said this.

It was said: falsehood is Satan, meaning he cannot add to it or subtract from it.

It was said: nothing is added to it or subtracted from it, neither by Jibril nor by Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿A revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy.﴾ This is a predicate for an omitted subject (mubtada', subject), or another attribute of "Book" according to those who allow placing a non-explicit attribute before an explicit one. It was also said that it is the attribute of "Book," and the clause "falsehood cannot approach it" is parenthetical between the described noun and its attribute.

Then God, glory be to Him, consoled His Messenger (ﷺ) regarding what he was affected by in terms of harm from the disbelievers, saying: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you.﴾ That is: what these disbelievers say to you, of describing you as a sorcerer, a liar, and a madman, is only like what was said to the messengers before you, for their peoples used to say to them the same as what these people say to you. It was also said: the meaning is: nothing is said to you of monotheism and sincerity of worship to God except what was said to the messengers before you, for all the sharia agree on this. It was also said that it is an interrogative, meaning: what is it that is said to you, except what was said to the messengers before you? ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness﴾ toward whoever deserves His forgiveness from among the monotheists who pledged allegiance to you and to those prophets before you, ﴿and full of painful punishment﴾ for the disbelievers who denied and opposed the messengers of God. It was also said: He is full of forgiveness toward the prophets, and full of punishment toward their enemies.

﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an,﴾ that is: if We had made the Qur'an that you recite to the people in a language other than Arabic, ﴿they would have said: "Why are its verses not explained?"﴾ That is: made clear in our language, for we are Arabs who do not understand the language of non-Arabs. The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Is it non-Arabic and Arabic?﴾ is for denial, and it is part of the speech of the polytheists, meaning: they would have said: "Is the speech non-Arabic and the messenger Arab?" A-'ajami (non-Arabic) is one who does not speak clearly, whether he is from the Arabs or the non-Arabs. Al-a'jam is the opposite of eloquent, meaning one who does not express his speech clearly, and an animal that does not speak is also called a'jam.

Abu Bakr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read: "a-a'jamiyyun" with two clear hamzas. al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya, Nasr ibn 'Asim, and Hisham read with one hamza as a statement. The rest read with the second hamza softened between two sounds. It was also said: the meaning is: "Why were its verses not explained, so that some of them would be non-Arabic to make non-Arabs understand, and some Arabic to make Arabs understand?"

Then God, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them, saying: ﴿Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing."﴾ That is: they are guided by it to the truth and are healed by it from every doubt and misgiving, and from illnesses and pains. ﴿And as for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness﴾ that is, deafness to hearing it and understanding its meanings, and for this reason they agreed to talk idly during it. ﴿And it is blindness upon them.﴾ Qatada said: they were blind to the Qur'an and deaf to it.

Al-Suddi said: their hearts became blind to it. The meaning is: it is for them a blindness, or it is described by the verbal noun for emphasis. The relative pronoun in His saying ﴿And those who do not believe﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is ﴿in their ears is deafness,﴾ or the second relative pronoun is conjoined to the first relative pronoun, and "deafness" is conjoined to "guidance" according to those who allow conjunction between two different governing words. The implied meaning is: it is guidance and healing for the first group, and deafness in their ears for the latter group.

Al-Jumhur read "'aman" with a fatha on the mim and tanwin, as a verbal noun. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, 'Amr ibn al-'As, and Ibn 'Umar read it with a kasra on the mim and tanwin, as a defective noun (ism manqus), described by it figuratively. 'Amr ibn Dinar read it with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the ya', as a past verb. Abu 'Ubayda preferred the first reading because of His earlier saying, "guidance and healing," and He did not say "guiding and healing." It was also said: the meaning is: "and the deafness upon them is blindness," and the indication of His saying "those" refers to those who do not believe and what is within their scope, and its predicate is ﴿They are called from a distant place,﴾ likening their condition, in terms of their not understanding the Qur'an, to the condition of one who is called from a far distance and cannot hear the voice of the one calling him from it.

Al-Farra' said: you say to the man who does not understand your speech: "You are being called from a distant place."

Al-Dahhak said: they will be called on the Day of Resurrection by their most despised names, from a distant place. Mujahid said: "from a distant place" means from their hearts.

Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related through the chain of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to prostrate at the last of the two verses of Ha Mim al-Sajda, while Ibn Mas'ud used to prostrate at the first of them.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abi Shayba related through the chain of Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar that he used to prostrate at the first.

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from him that he used to prostrate at the last verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs﴾ that he said: it is placing speech in other than its proper place.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him concerning His saying ﴿Is he who is thrown into the Fire﴾ (p-1319) that he said: "It is Abu Jahl ibn Hisham," and ﴿or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection﴾ that he said: "It is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Bashir ibn Tamim who said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahm and 'Ammar ibn Yasir. Ibn 'Asakir related the same from 'Ikrima.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Do what you will﴾ that he said: "This is specifically for the people of Badr."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an,﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "If We had made the Qur'an non-Arabic, and your tongue, O Muhammad, is Arabic, they would have said: 'Non-Arabic and Arabic! He brings it to us varied or mixed.' ﴿Why are its verses not explained?﴾ Why were its verses not made clear so that the Qur'an would be like the tongue?" He says: so We did not do that, lest they say it, and it would have been an argument against them.

He says: so We did not do that, lest they say it, and it would have been an argument against them.

It was said that the place of prostration is at His saying: ﴿If it is Him you worship,﴾ because it is connected to the command. It was said that it is at His saying: ﴿and they do not tire,﴾ because it completes the speech.

﴿So if they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord glorify Him night and day, and they never tire.﴾ That is: if these people are arrogant towards compliance, then the angels continually glorify God, glory be to Him, night and day, and they never grow weary or slacken.

﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled.﴾ The address here is to everyone who is fit for it, or to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Khashi'a (humbled) means dry and barren.

It was said: it means the dusty ground that does not produce plants.

The meaning of "swells" is that it rises and increases before it grows, as Mujahid and others said. According to this, there is an inversion in the speech, and its order is: it swelled and stirred. He says: so We did not do that, lest they say it, and it would have been an argument against them.

This is the reason for singling out prostration for the prohibition. It was also said that the reason for singling it out is that it is one of the highest levels of worship. It was said that the place of prostration is at His saying: ﴿If it is Him you worship,﴾ because it is connected to the command. It was said that it is at His saying: ﴿and they do not tire,﴾ because it completes the speech.

﴿So if they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord glorify Him night and day, and they never tire.﴾ That is: if these people are arrogant towards compliance, then the angels continually glorify God, glory be to Him, night and day, and they never grow weary or slacken.

﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled.﴾ The address here is to everyone who is fit for it, or to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Khashi'a (humbled) means dry and barren.

It was said: it means the dusty ground that does not produce plants.

"You see him like the blade of a sword, quivering for the dew, when you find with the evil man no food."

The meaning of "swells" is that it rises and increases before it grows, as Mujahid and others said. According to this, there is an inversion in the speech, and its order is: it swelled and stirred. Ilhad (deviation) is inclining and turning aside, and from it comes the lahd in the grave, because its side is inclined to one direction. Ibn Zayd said: they associate partners (with God). ﴿They are not hidden from Us;﴾ rather, We know them and will repay them for what they do.
