Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an,﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "If We had made the Qur'an non-Arabic, and your tongue, O Muhammad, is Arabic, they would have said: 'Non-Arabic and Arabic! He brings it to us varied or mixed.' ﴿Why are its verses not explained?﴾ Why were its verses not made clear so that the Qur'an would be like the tongue?" He says: so We did not do that, lest they say it, and it would have been an argument against them.

His saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed concerning it﴾. This is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*, a new clause that begins a fresh statement), and it contains consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the distress he felt at his people's disbelief and their attacks on the Qur'an. He is told that this is an old custom among the nations of the messengers: they dispute the Books sent down to them. By "the Book" is meant the Torah (*al-Tawrah*), and the pronoun in "concerning it" refers back to it. It has also been said that it refers to Moses, but the first view is preferable.

﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, concerning the delaying of the punishment for those among your community who denied, as in His saying: ﴿But He defers them until an appointed term﴾ [al-Naml: 61; Fatir: 45], ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ by hastening the punishment for those among them who denied. ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾, that is, concerning your Book that was sent down to you, which is the Qur'an. The meaning of "disquieting doubt" (*shakk muraib*) is doubt that causes unease, or doubt that is severe.

It has been said that the intended people are the Jews, and that they are in a disquieting doubt concerning the Torah, but the first view is preferable.

﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self﴾, that is, whoever obeys Allah, believes in His Messenger, and does not deny them, the reward for that returns to him and its benefit is specific to him. ﴿And whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾, that is, the punishment for his evil is upon him and not upon anyone else. ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾, so He does not punish anyone except for his sin, and injustice never proceeds from Him toward anyone, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all﴾ [Yunus: 44]. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already passed in the commentary on Surat Al 'Imran at His saying: ﴿and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182], and also in Surat al-Anfal.

Then He, exalted is He, informed that knowledge of the Hour and the time of its establishment is known to none but Him. So He said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾. Therefore, when a question is asked about it, the one asked is obliged to refer its knowledge to Him and not to anyone else. It has been narrated that the polytheists said: "O Muhammad, if you are a prophet, then tell us when the Hour will come," and so this was revealed. The "mā" in His saying ﴿And no fruits emerge from their sheaths﴾ is negative (*nafiyah*). The first "min" (in "min thamarat") is for comprehensiveness (*li-l-istighraq*, indicating all of the class), and the second "min" (in "min akmamiha") is for the beginning of the extent (*li-ibtida' al-ghayah*). It has also been said that "mā" is relative (*mawsulah*) in a position of genitive, conjoined to "the Hour", meaning: the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of what emerges. But the first view is preferable.

"Akmam" is the plural of *kimm*, with a kasra on the kaf, which is the covering of the fruit, and it is applied to every container for property or other things.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Its *akmam* are its coverings, and they are that in which the fruit is; its singular is *kimm* and *kimmah*."

Al-Raghib said: "The *kumm* is what covers the hand of a shirt, and what covers the fruit; its plural is *akmam*." This indicates that *kumm* with a damma on the kaf is used, because he made it shared between the sleeve of a shirt and the covering of a fruit, and there is no disagreement that the sleeve of a shirt is with a damma.

It may be said that the *kimm* which is the covering of fruit has two dialects.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *min thamarah* in the singular, while Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿Nor does any female conceive or give birth except with His knowledge﴾, that is: no female bears a pregnancy in her womb, and she does not deliver that pregnancy except with the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. The exception here is an *istithna' mufarragh* (an exceptive construction lacking its stated complement), taken from the most general of states; that is, nothing occurs of the emergence of a fruit, nor the bearing of one who bears, nor the delivery of one who delivers, in any state, except that it occurs with the knowledge of Allah. Therefore, the knowledge of the Hour is referred to Him, just as the knowledge of these matters is referred to Him.

﴿And the Day He will call to them﴾, that is, Allah, exalted is He, will call the polytheists, and that is the Day of Resurrection. He will say to them: ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, those whom you claimed in the world were My partners, from among the idols and others. ﴿Call upon them now, so that they may intercede for you or ward off the punishment from you.﴾ This is in the manner of mockery toward them.

The majority read *shurakā'iya* with the yā' sukūn (silent), while Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' fatḥah (vowelled). The governing element for "the Day" (*yawma*) is omitted; the meaning is: "Remember." ﴿They will say: "We have informed You that none of us bears witness."﴾ One says *ādhana yu'dhinu* when he informs, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Asma' has informed us of her parting, many a sojourner from whom the staying grows wearisome."

The meaning is: "We have informed You that none of us bears witness that You have a partner." That is because when they witnessed the Resurrection, they disowned the partners, and those idols that they used to worship disowned them.

It has been said that the one who says this is the objects of worship that they used to worship, meaning: "None of us is a witness who testifies that they were correct." But the first view is preferable.

﴿And what they used to call upon before has strayed from them﴾, that is: in the Hereafter, what they used to worship in the world, of idols and the like, has vanished and become void. ﴿And they will think that there is for them no place of escape﴾, that is, they became certain and knew that there is no escape for them. It is said: *hāṣa yaḥīṣu ḥaysan* when he fled.

It has been said that "thought" (*zann*) keeps its real meaning (*al-haqiqi*), because in those circumstances there remained in them a suspicion and a hope; but the first view is preferable.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned some conditions of man, so He said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾, that is, he does not weary of asking for good for himself and bringing it to himself. And "good" here means wealth, health, authority, and elevated status.

Al-Suddi said: "Man here is intended to mean the disbeliever." It has been said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; it has been said: 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf.

The better view is to take the verse in its generality according to what is most common, so the exclusion of the sincere servants does not contradict it.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "Man does not tire of asking for wealth."

﴿But if evil touches him, he is despairing and utterly hopeless﴾, that is: if calamity, hardship, poverty, or sickness touches him, he is despairing of the mercy of Allah and utterly hopeless of His compassion.

It has been said: he despairs of the answer to his supplication and is utterly hopeless from bad opinion of his Lord.

It has been said: he despairs of the removal of what is disliked that he has, and is utterly hopeless because of the thought that it will last. These two are intensive forms (*sighatā mubālaghah*), indicating that he is extremely despairing and greatly hopeless.

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him﴾, that is: if We give him good, well-being, and wealth after severity, sickness, and poverty, ﴿he will surely say: "This is mine"﴾, that is: this is something I deserve from Allah because of His approval of my deed. So he thinks that the blessing he has come into reached him by his deserving it, and he does not know that Allah tests His servants with good and evil, so that the grateful is distinguished from the ungrateful, and the patient from the impatient.

Mujahid said: "Its meaning: 'This is due to my deed, and I am entitled to it.'" ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, that is: I do not think it will occur as the prophets inform us, or: I am not certain of resurrection. This is specific to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Thus the intended "man" mentioned at the beginning of the verse is the category, according to the majority of its individuals, because despair of the mercy of Allah, hopelessness regarding His goodness, and doubt about resurrection occur only from disbelievers or from those wavering in religion who display Islam while concealing disbelief. ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾, on the assumption that what the prophets inform us of is true, of the establishment of the Hour and the occurrence of resurrection and rising, ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾, that is: the best condition of honour. So he thinks he deserves the good of this world because of the good in him, and deserves the good of the Hereafter because of what he believed about himself and affirmed for it; and this is a false belief and a corrupt assumption.

﴿Then We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, that is: We will inform them of it on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, a harsh one because of their sins. This *lam* and the one before it are *al-mu'attiyah li-l-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath).

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, that is, upon this category according to the majority of its individuals, ﴿he turns away﴾ from gratitude. ﴿And turns aside with his side﴾, that is: he rises above submission to the truth, and becomes proud and domineering. The word "side" here is *majaz* (figurative) for the self. It is said: *na'aytu* and *tana'aytu*, meaning: I went far and distanced myself, and *al-mun'ta*: the far place. From it is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"Indeed you are like the night which will overtake me, even though I think that the far place from you is wide."

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read *wa-nā'a bi-janibihi* with an alif before the hamza.

﴿But when evil touches him﴾, that is: affliction, exertion, poverty, or sickness, ﴿then he has much supplication﴾, that is: abundant. The Arabs use length and breadth figuratively for abundance; it is said: "So-and-so lengthened his speech" and "widened his supplication" when he increased it. The meaning: when evil touches him he humbles himself before Allah and seeks His help that He remove what has descended upon him, and he increases this. He remembers Him in hardship and forgets Him in ease; he calls upon Him when vengeance descends and abandons Him when blessing arrives. This is the practice of the disbelievers and of whoever among the Muslims is not firm of foot.

Then He, exalted is He, returned to addressing the disbelievers and disputing with them, so He said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered?"﴾, that is: inform me. ﴿If it is from Allah﴾, that is: the Qur'an, ﴿and you have disbelieved in it﴾, that is: you denied it, did not accept it, and did not act upon what is in it, ﴿who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾, that is: there is none more astray than you because of the extremity of your wretchedness and the severity of your hostility. The original form is: "What thing is more astray than you?", so ﴿one who is in opposition﴾ was placed in the position of the pronoun, to explain their state of opposition and that it is the greatest cause of their going astray.

﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾, that is: We will show them the indications of the truth of the Qur'an and the signs that it is from Allah, in the horizons ﴿and within themselves﴾. *Al-afaq* is the plural of *ufuq*, which means region. *Al-ufuq* with a damma on the hamza and fa', and so the lexicographers said. Al-Raghib related that it is said *afaq* with a fatha on both. The meaning: We will show them Our signs in the regions and within themselves, the events of the earth.

Mujahid said: "In the horizons: the conquest of the towns which Allah facilitated for His Messenger and for the caliphs after him and the helpers of His religion, in the horizons of the world east and west, and the triumph over the tyrants and the Chosroes. And within themselves: the conquest of Makkah." Ibn Jarir preferred this view.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "In the horizons: the battles of Allah among the nations; and within themselves: on the Day of Badr."

'Ata' said: "In the horizons: meaning the regions of the heavens and the earth, of the sun, moon, stars, night and day, winds, rains, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, plants, trees, mountains, seas, and other things. And within themselves: of subtle craftsmanship and wondrous wisdom, as in His saying: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]."

﴿Until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It has been said: it refers to Islam, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought to them. It has been said: it refers to what Allah shows them and does of that. It has been said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he is the true Messenger from Allah. But the first view is preferable.

﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is over all things a witness?﴾ The sentence is directed toward rebuking and reproaching them, and "concerning your Lord" is in the position of nominative, as the agent of *yakfi* (suffices); the *bā'* is redundant (*zā'idah*), and "that He" is a substitute (*badal*) for "your Lord." The hamza is for denial.

The meaning: Has it not sufficed them, instead of the promised signs that clarify the truth of the Qur'an, that He, exalted is He, is a witness over all things?

It has been said: the meaning is: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord, O Muhammad, that He is a witness over the deeds of the disbelievers?

It has been said: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord as a witness that the Qur'an is sent down from Him? *Al-Shahid* here means the Knowing, or it means the testimony which is presence.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of the implicit statement (*al-kinayah*) here is that Allah, mighty and majestic, has made clear to them what has sufficient proof in indication. The meaning: Has it not sufficed your Lord that He is over all things a witness, witnessing things, from which nothing is hidden?"

﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾, that is: in doubt about the resurrection, the reckoning, the reward, and the punishment. ﴿Unquestionably, He is all-encompassing of everything﴾: His knowledge encompasses all the known things, and His power encompasses all the things within capability. It is said: *aḥāṭa yuḥīṭu iḥāṭatan wa-ḥīṭatan*. In this is a severe warning, because one who encompasses everything such that nothing is hidden from Him recompenses the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾: "A term and a fixed time preceded for them from Allah, which they will reach."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And no fruits emerge from their sheaths﴾: "When it emerges."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verse 45–54 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿āqadhnāka﴾ (We have informed You): he said, "We have informed you."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿lā yasʾamu al-insānu﴾ (man does not tire of): he said, "He does not grow weary."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿sanuriyhim āyātinā fī al-āfāqi﴾ (We will show them Our signs in the horizons): he said, "Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding the verse: "What Allah opens of the towns." ﴿wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (and within themselves): he said, "The conquest of Makkah."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse: he said, "He withheld the rain from the whole earth." ﴿wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (and within themselves): he said, "The afflictions that occur in their bodies."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse: he said, "They used to travel and see the traces of ʿAd and Thamud, and they would say: 'By Allah, Muhammad has spoken the truth.'" And "What I do not see in themselves": he said, "The diseases."

He remembers Him in hardship and forgets Him in ease; he calls upon Him when vengeance descends and abandons Him when blessing arrives. Then He, exalted is He, returned to addressing the disbelievers and disputing with them, so He said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered?"﴾, that is: inform me. ﴿If it is from Allah﴾, that is: the Qur'an, ﴿and you have disbelieved in it﴾, that is: you denied it, did not accept it, and did not act upon what is in it, ﴿who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾, that is: there is none more astray than you because of the extremity of your wretchedness and the severity of your hostility. The original form is: "What thing is more astray than you?", so ﴿one who is in opposition﴾ was placed in the position of the pronoun, to explain their state of opposition and that it is the greatest cause of their going astray.

﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾, that is: We will show them the indications of the truth of the Qur'an and the signs that it is from Allah, in the horizons ﴿and within themselves﴾. *Al-afaq* is the plural of *ufuq*, which means region. *Al-ufuq* with a damma on the hamza and fa', and so the lexicographers said. Al-Raghib related that it is said *afaq* with a fatha on both. The meaning: We will show them Our signs in the regions and within themselves, the events of the earth.

Mujahid said: "In the horizons: the conquest of the towns which Allah facilitated for His Messenger and for the caliphs after him and the helpers of His religion, in the horizons of the world east and west, and the triumph over the tyrants and the Chosroes. And within themselves: the conquest of Makkah." Ibn Jarir preferred this view.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "In the horizons: the battles of Allah among the nations; and within themselves: on the Day of Badr."

'Ata' said: "In the horizons: meaning the regions of the heavens and the earth, of the sun, moon, stars, night and day, winds, rains, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, plants, trees, mountains, seas, and other things. And within themselves: of subtle craftsmanship and wondrous wisdom, as in His saying: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]."

﴿Until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It has been said: it refers to Islam, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought to them. It has been said: it refers to what Allah shows them and does of that. It has been said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he is the true Messenger from Allah. But the first view is preferable.

﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is over all things a witness?﴾ The sentence is directed toward rebuking and reproaching them, and "concerning your Lord" is in the position of nominative, as the agent of *yakfi* (suffices); the *bā'* is redundant (*zā'idah*), and "that He" is a substitute (*badal*) for "your Lord." The hamza is for denial.

The meaning: Has it not sufficed them, instead of the promised signs that clarify the truth of the Qur'an, that He, exalted is He, is a witness over all things?

It has been said: the meaning is: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord, O Muhammad, that He is a witness over the deeds of the disbelievers?

It has been said: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord as a witness that the Qur'an is sent down from Him? *Al-Shahid* here means the Knowing, or it means the testimony which is presence.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of the implicit statement (*al-kinayah*) here is that Allah, mighty and majestic, has made clear to them what has sufficient proof in indication. The meaning: Has it not sufficed your Lord that He is over all things a witness, witnessing things, from which nothing is hidden?"

﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾, that is: in doubt about the resurrection, the reckoning, the reward, and the punishment. ﴿Unquestionably, He is all-encompassing of everything﴾: His knowledge encompasses all the known things, and His power encompasses all the things within capability. It is said: *aḥāṭa yuḥīṭu iḥāṭatan wa-ḥīṭatan*. In this is a severe warning, because one who encompasses everything such that nothing is hidden from Him recompenses the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾: "A term and a fixed time preceded for them from Allah, which they will reach."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And no fruits emerge from their sheaths﴾: "When it emerges."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verse 45–54 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿āqadhnāka﴾ (We have informed You): he said, "We have informed you."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿lā yasʾamu al-insānu﴾ (man does not tire of): he said, "He does not grow weary."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿sanuriyhim āyātinā fī al-āfāqi﴾ (We will show them Our signs in the horizons): he said, "Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding the verse: "What Allah opens of the towns." ﴿wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (and within themselves): he said, "The conquest of Makkah."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse: he said, "He withheld the rain from the whole earth." ﴿wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (and within themselves): he said, "The afflictions that occur in their bodies."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse: he said, "They used to travel and see the traces of ʿAd and Thamud, and they would say: 'By Allah, Muhammad has spoken the truth.'" And "What I do not see in themselves": he said, "The diseases."

His saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed concerning it﴾. This is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*, a new clause that begins a fresh statement), and it contains consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the distress he felt at his people's disbelief and their attacks on the Qur'an. He is told that this is an old custom among the nations of the messengers: they dispute the Books sent down to them. By "the Book" is meant the Torah (*al-Tawrah*), and the pronoun in "concerning it" refers back to it. It has also been said that it refers to Moses, but the first view is preferable.

﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, concerning the delaying of the punishment for those among your community who denied, as in His saying: ﴿But He defers them until an appointed term﴾ [al-Naml: 61; Fatir: 45], ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ by hastening the punishment for those among them who denied. ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾, that is, concerning your Book that was sent down to you, which is the Qur'an. The meaning of "disquieting doubt" (*shakk muraib*) is doubt that causes unease, or doubt that is severe.

It has been said that the intended people are the Jews, and that they are in a disquieting doubt concerning the Torah, but the first view is preferable.

﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self﴾, that is, whoever obeys Allah, believes in His Messenger, and does not deny them, the reward for that returns to him and its benefit is specific to him. ﴿And whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾, that is, the punishment for his evil is upon him and not upon anyone else. ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾, so He does not punish anyone except for his sin, and injustice never proceeds from Him toward anyone, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all﴾ [Yunus: 44]. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already passed in the commentary on Surat Al 'Imran at His saying: ﴿and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182], and also in Surat al-Anfal.

Then He, exalted is He, informed that knowledge of the Hour and the time of its establishment is known to none but Him. So He said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾. Therefore, when a question is asked about it, the one asked is obliged to refer its knowledge to Him and not to anyone else. It has been narrated that the polytheists said: "O Muhammad, if you are a prophet, then tell us when the Hour will come," and so this was revealed. The "mā" in His saying ﴿And no fruits emerge from their sheaths﴾ is negative (*nafiyah*). The first "min" (in "min thamarat") is for comprehensiveness (*li-l-istighraq*, indicating all of the class), and the second "min" (in "min akmamiha") is for the beginning of the extent (*li-ibtida' al-ghayah*). It has also been said that "mā" is relative (*mawsulah*) in a position of genitive, conjoined to "the Hour", meaning: the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of what emerges. But the first view is preferable.

"Akmam" is the plural of *kimm*, with a kasra on the kaf, which is the covering of the fruit, and it is applied to every container for property or other things.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Its *akmam* are its coverings, and they are that in which the fruit is; its singular is *kimm* and *kimmah*."

Al-Raghib said: "The *kumm* is what covers the hand of a shirt, and what covers the fruit; its plural is *akmam*." This indicates that *kumm* with a damma on the kaf is used, because he made it shared between the sleeve of a shirt and the covering of a fruit, and there is no disagreement that the sleeve of a shirt is with a damma.

It may be said that the *kimm* which is the covering of fruit has two dialects.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *min thamarah* in the singular, while Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿Nor does any female conceive or give birth except with His knowledge﴾, that is: no female bears a pregnancy in her womb, and she does not deliver that pregnancy except with the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. The exception here is an *istithna' mufarragh* (an exceptive construction lacking its stated complement), taken from the most general of states; that is, nothing occurs of the emergence of a fruit, nor the bearing of one who bears, nor the delivery of one who delivers, in any state, except that it occurs with the knowledge of Allah. Therefore, the knowledge of the Hour is referred to Him, just as the knowledge of these matters is referred to Him.

﴿And the Day He will call to them﴾, that is, Allah, exalted is He, will call the polytheists, and that is the Day of Resurrection. He will say to them: ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, those whom you claimed in the world were My partners, from among the idols and others. ﴿Call upon them now, so that they may intercede for you or ward off the punishment from you.﴾ This is in the manner of mockery toward them.

The majority read *shurakā'iya* with the yā' sukūn (silent), while Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' fatḥah (vowelled). The governing element for "the Day" (*yawma*) is omitted; the meaning is: "Remember." ﴿They will say: "We have informed You that none of us bears witness."﴾ One says *ādhana yu'dhinu* when he informs, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Asma' has informed us of her parting, many a sojourner from whom the staying grows wearisome."

The meaning is: "We have informed You that none of us bears witness that You have a partner." That is because when they witnessed the Resurrection, they disowned the partners, and those idols that they used to worship disowned them.

It has been said that the one who says this is the objects of worship that they used to worship, meaning: "None of us is a witness who testifies that they were correct." But the first view is preferable.

﴿And what they used to call upon before has strayed from them﴾, that is: in the Hereafter, what they used to worship in the world, of idols and the like, has vanished and become void. ﴿And they will think that there is for them no place of escape﴾, that is, they became certain and knew that there is no escape for them. It is said: *hāṣa yaḥīṣu ḥaysan* when he fled.

It has been said that "thought" (*zann*) keeps its real meaning (*al-haqiqi*), because in those circumstances there remained in them a suspicion and a hope; but the first view is preferable.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned some conditions of man, so He said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾, that is, he does not weary of asking for good for himself and bringing it to himself. And "good" here means wealth, health, authority, and elevated status.

Al-Suddi said: "Man here is intended to mean the disbeliever." It has been said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; it has been said: 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf.

The better view is to take the verse in its generality according to what is most common, so the exclusion of the sincere servants does not contradict it.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "Man does not tire of asking for wealth."

﴿But if evil touches him, he is despairing and utterly hopeless﴾, that is: if calamity, hardship, poverty, or sickness touches him, he is despairing of the mercy of Allah and utterly hopeless of His compassion.

It has been said: he despairs of the answer to his supplication and is utterly hopeless from bad opinion of his Lord.

It has been said: he despairs of the removal of what is disliked that he has, and is utterly hopeless because of the thought that it will last. These two are intensive forms (*sighatā mubālaghah*), indicating that he is extremely despairing and greatly hopeless.

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him﴾, that is: if We give him good, well-being, and wealth after severity, sickness, and poverty, ﴿he will surely say: "This is mine"﴾, that is: this is something I deserve from Allah because of His approval of my deed. So he thinks that the blessing he has come into reached him by his deserving it, and he does not know that Allah tests His servants with good and evil, so that the grateful is distinguished from the ungrateful, and the patient from the impatient.

Mujahid said: "Its meaning: 'This is due to my deed, and I am entitled to it.'" ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, that is: I do not think it will occur as the prophets inform us, or: I am not certain of resurrection. This is specific to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Thus the intended "man" mentioned at the beginning of the verse is the category, according to the majority of its individuals, because despair of the mercy of Allah, hopelessness regarding His goodness, and doubt about resurrection occur only from disbelievers or from those wavering in religion who display Islam while concealing disbelief. ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾, on the assumption that what the prophets inform us of is true, of the establishment of the Hour and the occurrence of resurrection and rising, ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾, that is: the best condition of honour. So he thinks he deserves the good of this world because of the good in him, and deserves the good of the Hereafter because of what he believed about himself and affirmed for it; and this is a false belief and a corrupt assumption.

﴿Then We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, that is: We will inform them of it on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, a harsh one because of their sins. This *lam* and the one before it are *al-mu'attiyah li-l-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath).

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, that is, upon this category according to the majority of its individuals, ﴿he turns away﴾ from gratitude. ﴿And turns aside with his side﴾, that is: he rises above submission to the truth, and becomes proud and domineering. The word "side" here is *majaz* (figurative) for the self. It is said: *na'aytu* and *tana'aytu*, meaning: I went far and distanced myself, and *al-mun'ta*: the far place. From it is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"Indeed you are like the night which will overtake me, even though I think that the far place from you is wide."

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read *wa-nā'a bi-janibihi* with an alif before the hamza.

﴿But when evil touches him﴾, that is: affliction, exertion, poverty, or sickness, ﴿then he has much supplication﴾, that is: abundant. The Arabs use length and breadth figuratively for abundance; it is said: "So-and-so lengthened his speech" and "widened his supplication" when he increased it. The meaning: when evil touches him he humbles himself before Allah and seeks His help that He remove what has descended upon him, and he increases this. He remembers Him in hardship and forgets Him in ease; he calls upon Him when vengeance descends and abandons Him when blessing arrives. This is the practice of the disbelievers and of whoever among the Muslims is not firm of foot.

Then He, exalted is He, returned to addressing the disbelievers and disputing with them, so He said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered?"﴾, that is: inform me. ﴿If it is from Allah﴾, that is: the Qur'an, ﴿and you have disbelieved in it﴾, that is: you denied it, did not accept it, and did not act upon what is in it, ﴿who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾, that is: there is none more astray than you because of the extremity of your wretchedness and the severity of your hostility. ﴿And what they used to call upon before has strayed from them﴾, that is: in the Hereafter, what they used to worship in the world, of idols and the like, has vanished and become void. ﴿And they will think that there is for them no place of escape﴾, that is, they became certain and knew that there is no escape for them. It is said: *hāṣa yaḥīṣu ḥaysan* when he fled.

It has been said that "thought" (*zann*) keeps its real meaning (*al-haqiqi*), because in those circumstances there remained in them a suspicion and a hope; but the first view is preferable.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned some conditions of man, so He said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾, that is, he does not weary of asking for good for himself and bringing it to himself. And "good" here means wealth, health, authority, and elevated status.

Al-Suddi said: "Man here is intended to mean the disbeliever." It has been said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; it has been said: 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf.

The better view is to take the verse in its generality according to what is most common, so the exclusion of the sincere servants does not contradict it.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "Man does not tire of asking for wealth."

﴿But if evil touches him, he is despairing and utterly hopeless﴾, that is: if calamity, hardship, poverty, or sickness touches him, he is despairing of the mercy of Allah and utterly hopeless of His compassion.

It has been said: he despairs of the answer to his supplication and is utterly hopeless from bad opinion of his Lord.

It has been said: he despairs of the removal of what is disliked that he has, and is utterly hopeless because of the thought that it will last. These two are intensive forms (*sighatā mubālaghah*), indicating that he is extremely despairing and greatly hopeless.

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him﴾, that is: if We give him good, well-being, and wealth after severity, sickness, and poverty, ﴿he will surely say: "This is mine"﴾, that is: this is something I deserve from Allah because of His approval of my deed. So he thinks that the blessing he has come into reached him by his deserving it, and he does not know that Allah tests His servants with good and evil, so that the grateful is distinguished from the ungrateful, and the patient from the impatient.

Mujahid said: "Its meaning: 'This is due to my deed, and I am entitled to it.'" ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, that is: I do not think it will occur as the prophets inform us, or: I am not certain of resurrection. This is specific to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Thus the intended "man" mentioned at the beginning of the verse is the category, according to the majority of its individuals, because despair of the mercy of Allah, hopelessness regarding His goodness, and doubt about resurrection occur only from disbelievers or from those wavering in religion who display Islam while concealing disbelief. ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾, on the assumption that what the prophets inform us of is true, of the establishment of the Hour and the occurrence of resurrection and rising, ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾, that is: the best condition of honour. So he thinks he deserves the good of this world because of the good in him, and deserves the good of the Hereafter because of what he believed about himself and affirmed for it; and this is a false belief and a corrupt assumption.

﴿Then We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, that is: We will inform them of it on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, a harsh one because of their sins. This *lam* and the one before it are *al-mu'attiyah li-l-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath).

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, that is, upon this category according to the majority of its individuals, ﴿he turns away﴾ from gratitude. ﴿And turns aside with his side﴾, that is: he rises above submission to the truth, and becomes proud and domineering. The word "side" here is *majaz* (figurative) for the self. It is said: *na'aytu* and *tana'aytu*, meaning: I went far and distanced myself, and *al-mun'ta*: the far place. From it is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"Indeed you are like the night which will overtake me, even though I think that the far place from you is wide."

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read *wa-nā'a bi-janibihi* with an alif before the hamza.

﴿But when evil touches him﴾, that is: affliction, exertion, poverty, or sickness, ﴿then he has much supplication﴾, that is: abundant. The Arabs use length and breadth figuratively for abundance; it is said: "So-and-so lengthened his speech" and "widened his supplication" when he increased it. The meaning: when evil touches him he humbles himself before Allah and seeks His help that He remove what has descended upon him, and he increases this. He remembers Him in hardship and forgets Him in ease; he calls upon Him when vengeance descends and abandons Him when blessing arrives. This is the practice of the disbelievers and of whoever among the Muslims is not firm of foot.

Then He, exalted is He, returned to addressing the disbelievers and disputing with them, so He said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered?"﴾, that is: inform me. ﴿If it is from Allah﴾, that is: the Qur'an, ﴿and you have disbelieved in it﴾, that is: you denied it, did not accept it, and did not act upon what is in it, ﴿who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾, that is: there is none more astray than you because of the extremity of your wretchedness and the severity of your hostility. The original form is: "What thing is more astray than you?", so ﴿one who is in opposition﴾ was placed in the position of the pronoun, to explain their state of opposition and that it is the greatest cause of their going astray.

﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾, that is: We will show them the indications of the truth of the Qur'an and the signs that it is from Allah, in the horizons ﴿and within themselves﴾. *Al-afaq* is the plural of *ufuq*, which means region. *Al-ufuq* with a damma on the hamza and fa', and so the lexicographers said. Al-Raghib related that it is said *afaq* with a fatha on both. The meaning: We will show them Our signs in the regions and within themselves, the events of the earth.

Mujahid said: "In the horizons: the conquest of the towns which Allah facilitated for His Messenger and for the caliphs after him and the helpers of His religion, in the horizons of the world east and west, and the triumph over the tyrants and the Chosroes. And within themselves: the conquest of Makkah." Ibn Jarir preferred this view.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "In the horizons: the battles of Allah among the nations; and within themselves: on the Day of Badr."

'Ata' said: "In the horizons: meaning the regions of the heavens and the earth, of the sun, moon, stars, night and day, winds, rains, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, plants, trees, mountains, seas, and other things. And within themselves: of subtle craftsmanship and wondrous wisdom, as in His saying: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]."

﴿Until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It has been said: it refers to Islam, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought to them. It has been said: it refers to what Allah shows them and does of that. It has been said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he is the true Messenger from Allah. But the first view is preferable.

﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is over all things a witness?﴾ The sentence is directed toward rebuking and reproaching them, and "concerning your Lord" is in the position of nominative, as the agent of *yakfi* (suffices); the *bā'* is redundant (*zā'idah*), and "that He" is a substitute (*badal*) for "your Lord." The hamza is for denial.

The meaning: Has it not sufficed them, instead of the promised signs that clarify the truth of the Qur'an, that He, exalted is He, is a witness over all things?

It has been said: the meaning is: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord, O Muhammad, that He is a witness over the deeds of the disbelievers?

It has been said: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord as a witness that the Qur'an is sent down from Him? *Al-Shahid* here means the Knowing, or it means the testimony which is presence.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of the implicit statement (*al-kinayah*) here is that Allah, mighty and majestic, has made clear to them what has sufficient proof in indication. The meaning: Has it not sufficed your Lord that He is over all things a witness, witnessing things, from which nothing is hidden?"

﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾, that is: in doubt about the resurrection, the reckoning, the reward, and the punishment. ﴿Unquestionably, He is all-encompassing of everything﴾: His knowledge encompasses all the known things, and His power encompasses all the things within capability. It is said: *aḥāṭa yuḥīṭu iḥāṭatan wa-ḥīṭatan*. In this is a severe warning, because one who encompasses everything such that nothing is hidden from Him recompenses the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾: "A term and a fixed time preceded for them from Allah, which they will reach."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And no fruits emerge from their sheaths﴾: "When it emerges."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verse 45–54 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿āqadhnāka﴾ (We have informed You): he said, "We have informed you."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿sanuriyhim āyātinā fī al-āfāqi﴾ (We will show them Our signs in the horizons): he said, "Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding the verse: "What Allah opens of the towns." ﴿wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (and within themselves): he said, "The conquest of Makkah."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse: he said, "He withheld the rain from the whole earth." ﴿wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (and within themselves): he said, "The afflictions that occur in their bodies."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse: he said, "They used to travel and see the traces of ʿAd and Thamud, and they would say: 'By Allah, Muhammad has spoken the truth.'" And "What I do not see in themselves": he said, "The diseases."

His saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed concerning it﴾. This is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*, a new clause that begins a fresh statement), and it contains consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the distress he felt at his people's disbelief and their attacks on the Qur'an. He is told that this is an old custom among the nations of the messengers: they dispute the Books sent down to them. By "the Book" is meant the Torah (*al-Tawrah*), and the pronoun in "concerning it" refers back to it. It has also been said that it refers to Moses, but the first view is preferable.

﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, concerning the delaying of the punishment for those among your community who denied, as in His saying: ﴿But He defers them until an appointed term﴾ [al-Naml: 61; Fatir: 45], ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ by hastening the punishment for those among them who denied. ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾, that is, concerning your Book that was sent down to you, which is the Qur'an. The meaning of "disquieting doubt" (*shakk muraib*) is doubt that causes unease, or doubt that is severe.

It has been said that the intended people are the Jews, and that they are in a disquieting doubt concerning the Torah, but the first view is preferable.

﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self﴾, that is, whoever obeys Allah, believes in His Messenger, and does not deny them, the reward for that returns to him and its benefit is specific to him. ﴿And whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾, that is, the punishment for his evil is upon him and not upon anyone else. ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾, so He does not punish anyone except for his sin, and injustice never proceeds from Him toward anyone, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all﴾ [Yunus: 44]. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already passed in the commentary on Surat Al 'Imran at His saying: ﴿and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182], and also in Surat al-Anfal.

Then He, exalted is He, informed that knowledge of the Hour and the time of its establishment is known to none but Him. So He said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾. Therefore, when a question is asked about it, the one asked is obliged to refer its knowledge to Him and not to anyone else. It has been narrated that the polytheists said: "O Muhammad, if you are a prophet, then tell us when the Hour will come," and so this was revealed. The "mā" in His saying ﴿And no fruits emerge from their sheaths﴾ is negative (*nafiyah*). The first "min" (in "min thamarat") is for comprehensiveness (*li-l-istighraq*, indicating all of the class), and the second "min" (in "min akmamiha") is for the beginning of the extent (*li-ibtida' al-ghayah*). It has also been said that "mā" is relative (*mawsulah*) in a position of genitive, conjoined to "the Hour", meaning: the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of what emerges. But the first view is preferable.

"Akmam" is the plural of *kimm*, with a kasra on the kaf, which is the covering of the fruit, and it is applied to every container for property or other things.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Its *akmam* are its coverings, and they are that in which the fruit is; its singular is *kimm* and *kimmah*."

Al-Raghib said: "The *kumm* is what covers the hand of a shirt, and what covers the fruit; its plural is *akmam*." This indicates that *kumm* with a damma on the kaf is used, because he made it shared between the sleeve of a shirt and the covering of a fruit, and there is no disagreement that the sleeve of a shirt is with a damma.

It may be said that the *kimm* which is the covering of fruit has two dialects.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *min thamarah* in the singular, while Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿Nor does any female conceive or give birth except with His knowledge﴾, that is: no female bears a pregnancy in her womb, and she does not deliver that pregnancy except with the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. The exception here is an *istithna' mufarragh* (an exceptive construction lacking its stated complement), taken from the most general of states; that is, nothing occurs of the emergence of a fruit, nor the bearing of one who bears, nor the delivery of one who delivers, in any state, except that it occurs with the knowledge of Allah. Therefore, the knowledge of the Hour is referred to Him, just as the knowledge of these matters is referred to Him.

﴿And the Day He will call to them﴾, that is, Allah, exalted is He, will call the polytheists, and that is the Day of Resurrection. He will say to them: ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, those whom you claimed in the world were My partners, from among the idols and others. ﴿Call upon them now, so that they may intercede for you or ward off the punishment from you.﴾ This is in the manner of mockery toward them.

The majority read *shurakā'iya* with the yā' sukūn (silent), while Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' fatḥah (vowelled). The governing element for "the Day" (*yawma*) is omitted; the meaning is: "Remember." ﴿They will say: "We have informed You that none of us bears witness."﴾ One says *ādhana yu'dhinu* when he informs, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Asma' has informed us of her parting, many a sojourner from whom the staying grows wearisome."

The meaning is: "We have informed You that none of us bears witness that You have a partner." That is because when they witnessed the Resurrection, they disowned the partners, and those idols that they used to worship disowned them.

It has been said that the one who says this is the objects of worship that they used to worship, meaning: "None of us is a witness who testifies that they were correct." But the first view is preferable.

﴿And what they used to call upon before has strayed from them﴾, that is: in the Hereafter, what they used to worship in the world, of idols and the like, has vanished and become void. ﴿And they will think that there is for them no place of escape﴾, that is, they became certain and knew that there is no escape for them. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned some conditions of man, so He said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾, that is, he does not weary of asking for good for himself and bringing it to himself. And "good" here means wealth, health, authority, and elevated status.

The better view is to take the verse in its generality according to what is most common, so the exclusion of the sincere servants does not contradict it.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "Man does not tire of asking for wealth."

﴿But if evil touches him, he is despairing and utterly hopeless﴾, that is: if calamity, hardship, poverty, or sickness touches him, he is despairing of the mercy of Allah and utterly hopeless of His compassion.

It has been said: he despairs of the answer to his supplication and is utterly hopeless from bad opinion of his Lord.

It has been said: he despairs of the removal of what is disliked that he has, and is utterly hopeless because of the thought that it will last. These two are intensive forms (*sighatā mubālaghah*), indicating that he is extremely despairing and greatly hopeless.

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him﴾, that is: if We give him good, well-being, and wealth after severity, sickness, and poverty, ﴿he will surely say: "This is mine"﴾, that is: this is something I deserve from Allah because of His approval of my deed. So he thinks that the blessing he has come into reached him by his deserving it, and he does not know that Allah tests His servants with good and evil, so that the grateful is distinguished from the ungrateful, and the patient from the impatient.

Mujahid said: "Its meaning: 'This is due to my deed, and I am entitled to it.'" ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, that is: I do not think it will occur as the prophets inform us, or: I am not certain of resurrection. This is specific to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Thus the intended "man" mentioned at the beginning of the verse is the category, according to the majority of its individuals, because despair of the mercy of Allah, hopelessness regarding His goodness, and doubt about resurrection occur only from disbelievers or from those wavering in religion who display Islam while concealing disbelief. ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾, on the assumption that what the prophets inform us of is true, of the establishment of the Hour and the occurrence of resurrection and rising, ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾, that is: the best condition of honour. So he thinks he deserves the good of this world because of the good in him, and deserves the good of the Hereafter because of what he believed about himself and affirmed for it; and this is a false belief and a corrupt assumption.

﴿Then We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, that is: We will inform them of it on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, a harsh one because of their sins. This *lam* and the one before it are *al-mu'attiyah li-l-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath).

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, that is, upon this category according to the majority of its individuals, ﴿he turns away﴾ from gratitude. ﴿And turns aside with his side﴾, that is: he rises above submission to the truth, and becomes proud and domineering. He is told that this is an old custom among the nations of the messengers: they dispute the Books sent down to them. By "the Book" is meant the Torah (*al-Tawrah*), and the pronoun in "concerning it" refers back to it. It has also been said that it refers to Moses, but the first view is preferable.

﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, concerning the delaying of the punishment for those among your community who denied, as in His saying: ﴿But He defers them until an appointed term﴾ [al-Naml: 61; Fatir: 45], ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾ by hastening the punishment for those among them who denied. ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾, that is, concerning your Book that was sent down to you, which is the Qur'an. The meaning of "disquieting doubt" (*shakk muraib*) is doubt that causes unease, or doubt that is severe.

It has been said that the intended people are the Jews, and that they are in a disquieting doubt concerning the Torah, but the first view is preferable.

﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self﴾, that is, whoever obeys Allah, believes in His Messenger, and does not deny them, the reward for that returns to him and its benefit is specific to him. ﴿And whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾, that is, the punishment for his evil is upon him and not upon anyone else. ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾, so He does not punish anyone except for his sin, and injustice never proceeds from Him toward anyone, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all﴾ [Yunus: 44]. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already passed in the commentary on Surat Al 'Imran at His saying: ﴿and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182], and also in Surat al-Anfal.

Then He, exalted is He, informed that knowledge of the Hour and the time of its establishment is known to none but Him. So He said: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾. Therefore, when a question is asked about it, the one asked is obliged to refer its knowledge to Him and not to anyone else. It has been narrated that the polytheists said: "O Muhammad, if you are a prophet, then tell us when the Hour will come," and so this was revealed. The "mā" in His saying ﴿And no fruits emerge from their sheaths﴾ is negative (*nafiyah*). The first "min" (in "min thamarat") is for comprehensiveness (*li-l-istighraq*, indicating all of the class), and the second "min" (in "min akmamiha") is for the beginning of the extent (*li-ibtida' al-ghayah*). It has also been said that "mā" is relative (*mawsulah*) in a position of genitive, conjoined to "the Hour", meaning: the knowledge of the Hour and the knowledge of what emerges. But the first view is preferable.

"Akmam" is the plural of *kimm*, with a kasra on the kaf, which is the covering of the fruit, and it is applied to every container for property or other things.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Its *akmam* are its coverings, and they are that in which the fruit is; its singular is *kimm* and *kimmah*."

Al-Raghib said: "The *kumm* is what covers the hand of a shirt, and what covers the fruit; its plural is *akmam*." This indicates that *kumm* with a damma on the kaf is used, because he made it shared between the sleeve of a shirt and the covering of a fruit, and there is no disagreement that the sleeve of a shirt is with a damma.

It may be said that the *kimm* which is the covering of fruit has two dialects.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *min thamarah* in the singular, while Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿Nor does any female conceive or give birth except with His knowledge﴾, that is: no female bears a pregnancy in her womb, and she does not deliver that pregnancy except with the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. The exception here is an *istithna' mufarragh* (an exceptive construction lacking its stated complement), taken from the most general of states; that is, nothing occurs of the emergence of a fruit, nor the bearing of one who bears, nor the delivery of one who delivers, in any state, except that it occurs with the knowledge of Allah. Therefore, the knowledge of the Hour is referred to Him, just as the knowledge of these matters is referred to Him.

﴿And the Day He will call to them﴾, that is, Allah, exalted is He, will call the polytheists, and that is the Day of Resurrection. He will say to them: ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, those whom you claimed in the world were My partners, from among the idols and others. ﴿Call upon them now, so that they may intercede for you or ward off the punishment from you.﴾ This is in the manner of mockery toward them.

The majority read *shurakā'iya* with the yā' sukūn (silent), while Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' fatḥah (vowelled). The governing element for "the Day" (*yawma*) is omitted; the meaning is: "Remember." ﴿They will say: "We have informed You that none of us bears witness."﴾ One says *ādhana yu'dhinu* when he informs, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Asma' has informed us of her parting, many a sojourner from whom the staying grows wearisome."

The meaning is: "We have informed You that none of us bears witness that You have a partner." That is because when they witnessed the Resurrection, they disowned the partners, and those idols that they used to worship disowned them.

It has been said that the one who says this is the objects of worship that they used to worship, meaning: "None of us is a witness who testifies that they were correct." But the first view is preferable.

﴿And what they used to call upon before has strayed from them﴾, that is: in the Hereafter, what they used to worship in the world, of idols and the like, has vanished and become void. ﴿And they will think that there is for them no place of escape﴾, that is, they became certain and knew that there is no escape for them. It is said: *hāṣa yaḥīṣu ḥaysan* when he fled.

It has been said that "thought" (*zann*) keeps its real meaning (*al-haqiqi*), because in those circumstances there remained in them a suspicion and a hope; but the first view is preferable.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned some conditions of man, so He said: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾, that is, he does not weary of asking for good for himself and bringing it to himself. And "good" here means wealth, health, authority, and elevated status.

Al-Suddi said: "Man here is intended to mean the disbeliever." It has been said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; it has been said: 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf.

The better view is to take the verse in its generality according to what is most common, so the exclusion of the sincere servants does not contradict it.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "Man does not tire of asking for wealth."

﴿But if evil touches him, he is despairing and utterly hopeless﴾, that is: if calamity, hardship, poverty, or sickness touches him, he is despairing of the mercy of Allah and utterly hopeless of His compassion.

It has been said: he despairs of the answer to his supplication and is utterly hopeless from bad opinion of his Lord.

It has been said: he despairs of the removal of what is disliked that he has, and is utterly hopeless because of the thought that it will last. These two are intensive forms (*sighatā mubālaghah*), indicating that he is extremely despairing and greatly hopeless.

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him﴾, that is: if We give him good, well-being, and wealth after severity, sickness, and poverty, ﴿he will surely say: "This is mine"﴾, that is: this is something I deserve from Allah because of His approval of my deed. So he thinks that the blessing he has come into reached him by his deserving it, and he does not know that Allah tests His servants with good and evil, so that the grateful is distinguished from the ungrateful, and the patient from the impatient.

Mujahid said: "Its meaning: 'This is due to my deed, and I am entitled to it.'" ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, that is: I do not think it will occur as the prophets inform us, or: I am not certain of resurrection. This is specific to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Thus the intended "man" mentioned at the beginning of the verse is the category, according to the majority of its individuals, because despair of the mercy of Allah, hopelessness regarding His goodness, and doubt about resurrection occur only from disbelievers or from those wavering in religion who display Islam while concealing disbelief. ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾, on the assumption that what the prophets inform us of is true, of the establishment of the Hour and the occurrence of resurrection and rising, ﴿indeed I will have with Him the best﴾, that is: the best condition of honour. So he thinks he deserves the good of this world because of the good in him, and deserves the good of the Hereafter because of what he believed about himself and affirmed for it; and this is a false belief and a corrupt assumption.

﴿Then We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾, that is: We will inform them of it on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾, a harsh one because of their sins. This *lam* and the one before it are *al-mu'attiyah li-l-qasam* (the lam that prepares for an oath).

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, that is, upon this category according to the majority of its individuals, ﴿he turns away﴾ from gratitude. ﴿And turns aside with his side﴾, that is: he rises above submission to the truth, and becomes proud and domineering. The word "side" here is *majaz* (figurative) for the self. It is said: *na'aytu* and *tana'aytu*, meaning: I went far and distanced myself, and *al-mun'ta*: the far place. From it is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"Indeed you are like the night which will overtake me, even though I think that the far place from you is wide."

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read *wa-nā'a bi-janibihi* with an alif before the hamza.

﴿But when evil touches him﴾, that is: affliction, exertion, poverty, or sickness, ﴿then he has much supplication﴾, that is: abundant. The Arabs use length and breadth figuratively for abundance; it is said: "So-and-so lengthened his speech" and "widened his supplication" when he increased it. The meaning: when evil touches him he humbles himself before Allah and seeks His help that He remove what has descended upon him, and he increases this. He remembers Him in hardship and forgets Him in ease; he calls upon Him when vengeance descends and abandons Him when blessing arrives. This is the practice of the disbelievers and of whoever among the Muslims is not firm of foot.

Then He, exalted is He, returned to addressing the disbelievers and disputing with them, so He said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered?"﴾, that is: inform me. ﴿If it is from Allah﴾, that is: the Qur'an, ﴿and you have disbelieved in it﴾, that is: you denied it, did not accept it, and did not act upon what is in it, ﴿who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾, that is: there is none more astray than you because of the extremity of your wretchedness and the severity of your hostility. The original form is: "What thing is more astray than you?", so ﴿one who is in opposition﴾ was placed in the position of the pronoun, to explain their state of opposition and that it is the greatest cause of their going astray.

﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾, that is: We will show them the indications of the truth of the Qur'an and the signs that it is from Allah, in the horizons ﴿and within themselves﴾. *Al-afaq* is the plural of *ufuq*, which means region. *Al-ufuq* with a damma on the hamza and fa', and so the lexicographers said. Al-Raghib related that it is said *afaq* with a fatha on both. The meaning: We will show them Our signs in the regions and within themselves, the events of the earth.

Mujahid said: "In the horizons: the conquest of the towns which Allah facilitated for His Messenger and for the caliphs after him and the helpers of His religion, in the horizons of the world east and west, and the triumph over the tyrants and the Chosroes. And within themselves: the conquest of Makkah." Ibn Jarir preferred this view.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "In the horizons: the battles of Allah among the nations; and within themselves: on the Day of Badr."

'Ata' said: "In the horizons: meaning the regions of the heavens and the earth, of the sun, moon, stars, night and day, winds, rains, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, plants, trees, mountains, seas, and other things. And within themselves: of subtle craftsmanship and wondrous wisdom, as in His saying: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]."

﴿Until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It has been said: it refers to Islam, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought to them. It has been said: it refers to what Allah shows them and does of that. It has been said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he is the true Messenger from Allah. But the first view is preferable.

﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is over all things a witness?﴾ The sentence is directed toward rebuking and reproaching them, and "concerning your Lord" is in the position of nominative, as the agent of *yakfi* (suffices); the *bā'* is redundant (*zā'idah*), and "that He" is a substitute (*badal*) for "your Lord." The hamza is for denial.

The meaning: Has it not sufficed them, instead of the promised signs that clarify the truth of the Qur'an, that He, exalted is He, is a witness over all things?

It has been said: the meaning is: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord, O Muhammad, that He is a witness over the deeds of the disbelievers?

It has been said: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord as a witness that the Qur'an is sent down from Him? *Al-Shahid* here means the Knowing, or it means the testimony which is presence.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of the implicit statement (*al-kinayah*) here is that Allah, mighty and majestic, has made clear to them what has sufficient proof in indication. The meaning: Has it not sufficed your Lord that He is over all things a witness, witnessing things, from which nothing is hidden?"

﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾, that is: in doubt about the resurrection, the reckoning, the reward, and the punishment. ﴿Unquestionably, He is all-encompassing of everything﴾: His knowledge encompasses all the known things, and His power encompasses all the things within capability. It is said: *aḥāṭa yuḥīṭu iḥāṭatan wa-ḥīṭatan*. In this is a severe warning, because one who encompasses everything such that nothing is hidden from Him recompenses the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾: "A term and a fixed time preceded for them from Allah, which they will reach."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And no fruits emerge from their sheaths﴾: "When it emerges."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 41, verse 45–54 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿āqadhnāka﴾ (We have informed You): he said, "We have informed you."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿lā yasʾamu al-insānu﴾ (man does not tire of): he said, "He does not grow weary."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿sanuriyhim āyātinā fī al-āfāqi﴾ (We will show them Our signs in the horizons): he said, "Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding the verse: "What Allah opens of the towns." ﴿wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (and within themselves): he said, "The conquest of Makkah."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse: he said, "He withheld the rain from the whole earth." ﴿wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (and within themselves): he said, "The afflictions that occur in their bodies."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse: he said, "They used to travel and see the traces of ʿAd and Thamud, and they would say: 'By Allah, Muhammad has spoken the truth.'" And "What I do not see in themselves": he said, "The diseases."

This is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*, a new clause that begins a fresh statement), and it contains consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the distress he felt at his people's disbelief and their attacks on the Qur'an. He is told that this is an old custom among the nations of the messengers: they dispute the Books sent down to them. By "the Book" is meant the Torah (*al-Tawrah*), and the pronoun in "concerning it" refers back to it. It has also been said that it refers to Moses, but the first view is preferable.

﴿Until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It has been said: it refers to Islam, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought to them. It has been said: it refers to what Allah shows them and does of that. It has been said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), that he is the true Messenger from Allah. But the first view is preferable.

The hamza is for denial.

The meaning: Has it not sufficed them, instead of the promised signs that clarify the truth of the Qur'an, that He, exalted is He, is a witness over all things?

It has been said: the meaning is: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord, O Muhammad, that He is a witness over the deeds of the disbelievers?

It has been said: Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord as a witness that the Qur'an is sent down from Him? *Al-Shahid* here means the Knowing, or it means the testimony which is presence.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of the implicit statement (*al-kinayah*) here is that Allah, mighty and majestic, has made clear to them what has sufficient proof in indication. The meaning: Has it not sufficed your Lord that He is over all things a witness, witnessing things, from which nothing is hidden?"

﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord﴾, that is: in doubt about the resurrection, the reckoning, the reward, and the punishment. ﴿Unquestionably, He is all-encompassing of everything﴾: His knowledge encompasses all the known things, and His power encompasses all the things within capability. It is said: *aḥāṭa yuḥīṭu iḥāṭatan wa-ḥīṭatan*. Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾: "A term and a fixed time preceded for them from Allah, which they will reach."
